## [Trudge through the New Year – My Diary by Cao Ou, Part I](https://artchinauk.com/trudge-through-the-new-year-my-diary-by-cao-ou-part-i/)

Our whole family drove back to my hometown in Shandong just five days before Chinese New Year’s Eve in 2020. We saw the news about Wuhan’s pneumonia on our phones. The report said it was not serious. I didn’t even watch the news and only heard a few words about it from the family.

![Image 121](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2019/12/Screenshot-2019-12-10-at-19.31.11.png)

My studio

We stopped a few times in the services on the highway during our journey. The services were busy, and nobody was wearing a mask. It surprised me how many people went back home much earlier, and there were not so many people around this time as in previous years. It usually gets crowded 2 days before the New Year. Normally this is a 12 hour journey,but it took us over 16 hours because of the traffic. It was ok for us, but my poor cat suffered as it couldn’t go to the toilet for the whole duration.

![Image 122](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/04/WechatIMG214.jpeg)My lovely cats

Since I hadn’t been home for two years, I went out for a drink with friends most nights before my departure. After we arrived at my parents’ home, Wuhan’s epidemic was getting worse. I watched the news and paid more attention to the situation.

I have a friend in Wuhan. So I chatted with him and asked him how it was there. He was shopping at the supermarket and was wearing a mask by then. There were many people in the supermarket. He said that the news of the epidemic was bad. However, people remained very relaxed. Life continued as normal,the epidemic seemed to be no big deal.

![Image 123](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/04/WechatIMG215.jpg)

My work used for this book’s cover.

At noon on New Year’s Day, our family was still eating out at a restaurant. On the next day, my city suddenly issued an emergency notice that all restaurants, shops, leisure centres, and other public places should close at once – this was mandatory. We lined up outside a shop and started buying masks. The medicine in the pharmacy was almost wiped out. Everyone bought hundreds of RMB worth of medicine to prepare for a long time staying at home. A mask was a few cents,so I bought a pack. The next day we remained at home. The first thing in the morning is to watch the news. We found the number of affected people had increased several times from the previous day. Two days later, all the residential districts were closed. Now you must wear a mask and measure your temperature when entering the residential district. At the beginning of New Year, from the first day to the fifteenth, is a time for families and friends to come together. H owever, everything had to be cancelled.

## [A Sketch of the Wuhan Epidemic](https://artchinauk.com/a-sketch-of-the-wuhan-epidemic/)

Words By Mu Beini at 31/03/2020, translated by Aimin Liu.

From the beginning of the epidemic to the end of January, Wuhan shut down the whole city. For me, life did not change that much as I paint and work mostly from home.

![Image 124](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/04/%E6%AD%A6%E6%B1%89%E7%B9%81%E5%8D%8E%E7%9A%84%E6%B1%89%E8%A1%97%E4%B8%8A%E7%A9%BA%E6%97%A0%E4%B8%80%E8%BD%A6%EF%BC%8C%E5%A4%A7%E5%AE%B6%E9%83%BD%E5%9C%A8%E9%9D%99%E9%9D%99%E7%AD%89%E5%BE%85.jpg)City of Wu Han, after shut down.

![Image 125](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/04/%E4%BB%A5%E5%BE%80%E7%B9%81%E5%BF%99%E7%9A%84%E6%AD%A6%E6%B1%89%E9%AB%98%E9%93%81%E7%AB%99%E5%86%85%E7%8E%B0%E5%9C%A8%E5%8F%AA%E6%9C%89%E5%B7%A5%E4%BD%9C%E4%BA%BA%E5%91%98%E5%9C%A8%E5%81%9A%E6%B6%88%E6%AF%92%E5%87%86%E5%A4%87%E5%B7%A5%E4%BD%9C%E4%BD%9C.jpg)Empty Bullet Train Station

Besides, I had previous experience of disasters, the Tohoku earthquake and the nuclear disaster in Japan in 2011. Following these events, I ended up at home for more than a month. With this previous experience, I felt very calm as we encountered the epidemic. My close friends would joke that I would be the last person to take the epidemic seriously. Also, maybe my character is more pessimistic. I believe in fate and that people’s lives and deaths are already pre-determined. Irrespective of whether you panic or not you will not change your fate. So, I would rather stay calm and work on how to protect my family and try to live fruitfully every single day. Fortunately, the simple pleasures of life in a small family of three makes my life quite satisfying and reassuring.

![Image 126](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/04/%E5%B0%8F%E5%8C%BA%E7%9A%84%E6%A4%8D%E7%89%A9%E9%95%BF%E7%9A%84%E5%BC%82%E5%B8%B8%E8%8C%82%E7%9B%9B%EF%BC%8C%E5%8F%AF%E6%98%AF%E6%97%A0%E4%BA%BA%E8%A7%82%E8%B5%8F.jpg)Overgrown communal garden in our residential district.

![Image 127](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/04/%E6%98%A5%E5%A4%A9%E5%A4%AA%E9%98%B3%E5%87%BA%E6%9D%A5%E4%BA%86%EF%BC%8C%E5%B0%8F%E5%8C%BA%E7%9A%84%E4%BA%BA%E4%BB%AC%E9%83%BD%E5%9C%A8%E9%98%B3%E5%8F%B0%E4%B8%8A%E6%99%92%E8%B5%B7%E8%A2%AB%E5%AD%90%E4%BA%86.jpg)Spring is here. When the sun came out, people in the flats took their quilts out on the balcony.

Since the residential district restrictions on people going out, the management of our building has been very responsible and well organised. Such as – there is a shopping platform for door-to-door delivery, distribution of free food, offers of postal services and haircuts and so on. My thanks go to those who have been working in the front line in property management, to the volunteers and the party members. I’m grateful in my heart for what I’ve seen and for what I’ve experienced. I broke into tears when I watched Chinese medical workers fighting with soldiers on the front line of Corvid-19 on TV. However, as an ordinary citizen, the only thing I could do to help was to stay at home.

![Image 128](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/04/%E7%96%AB%E6%83%85%E6%9C%9F%E9%97%B4%E6%AF%8F%E5%A4%A9%E5%9C%A8%E5%AE%B6%E7%94%BB%E7%94%BB%E3%80%81%E7%9C%8B%E4%B9%A6%E3%80%81%E5%88%B7%E6%89%8B%E6%9C%BA%EF%BC%8C%E6%84%9F%E8%A7%89%E5%92%8C%E5%B9%B3%E6%97%B6%E4%B9%9F%E6%B2%A1%E6%9C%89%E5%A4%AA%E5%A4%A7%E5%8F%98%E5%8C%96.jpg)During the epidemic, I draw pictures, read books and check my phone every day.

![Image 129](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/04/%E6%AF%8F%E5%A4%A9%E5%85%A8%E5%AE%B6%E4%B8%89%E5%8F%A3%E4%BA%BA%E5%92%8C%E7%8C%AB%E5%84%BF%E4%B8%80%E8%B5%B7%E5%91%86%E5%9C%A8%E5%AE%B6%E9%87%8C%E7%AD%89%E5%A4%8F%E5%A4%A9%EF%BC%8C%E5%B7%B2%E7%BB%8F%E8%BF%99%E6%A0%B7%E9%9D%99%E9%9D%99%E7%AD%89%E5%BE%85%E4%BA%862%E4%B8%AA%E6%9C%88%E5%A4%9A.jpg)Every day, the family of three stays at home with the cat and waits for the summer, and has been waiting quietly for more than 2 months.

During the epidemic, my students and I drew a set of fight-epidemic postcards for the Hubei Red Cross. These drawings have already been printed and should be published nationwide when the epidemic is over. They are the record I made during the epidemic and I hope they make a small mark in history.

![Image 130](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/04/%E6%AD%A6%E6%B1%89%E6%85%A2%E6%85%A2%E5%9C%A8%E8%A7%A3%E5%B0%81%EF%BC%8C%E9%AB%98%E9%93%81%E7%AB%99%E4%B9%9F%E5%9C%A8%E5%87%86%E5%A4%87%E8%BF%8E%E6%8E%A5%E8%A7%A3%E7%A6%81%E5%90%8E%E7%9A%84%E7%AC%AC%E4%B8%80%E6%89%B9%E5%AE%A2%E4%BA%BA.jpg)Wu Han’s train station welcome the first group of people since the epidemic broke out.

## [“Under the Mask of Us”: He Kun’s Response to the Coronavirus](https://artchinauk.com/under-the-mask-of-us-he-kuns-response-to-the-coronavirus/)

This week, we are going to talk about our artist He Kun’s latest ink painting series, titled “Under the Mask of Us”. This collection of work relates to the impact of the coronavirus on China and we are sharing as part of our ongoing project at present: “Art for Wuhan, China”.

1: “Under the Mask of Us”

![Image 132](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/03/640.jpeg)**Image:**_“We, They_”_, 33cm x 33cm, ink painting on Xuan paper_

You can’t see full faces under the masks, only sadness, kindness, and confident eyes. Masks cover us, all of the beautiful faces; who are you, who is she? These are no longer important questions. These are the ordinary, normal people under the masks, those of us who have taken on the responsibility to save lives.

![Image 133](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/03/640-3.jpg)

This is a group of portraits depicting medical staff specifically. The iInk paintings show us close-ups of people’s faces during this special period – people with masks. Masks are the only defence for them to fight this invisible virus; they know the risk is high, but they have chosen to help and save lives, despite whatever the cost may be to them.

![Image 134](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/03/640-1.jpeg)

In this painting from the series shown above, titled “We, They”, the strong black lines convey the contour of head and torso, the precise, free brushstrokes showing the artist’s confidence and how he incorporates the art of calligraphy into his painting. Through those strong outlines, he conveys the determination from our nurses and doctors. The changes in the tones of grey create beautiful texture in the hat, mask, and clothes. The background of each of these paintings is white, which symbolises that these medical professionals are our “White Angels”.

We always say that human eyes are the window to our soul; in each of He Kun’s portraits, the doctors and nurses wear a hat, mask, and hospital uniform. Only their eyes are naked in front of viewers. Can you see their sadness, kindness, hope, or hopelessness? Have they evoked your strongest emotion inside you? Have you felt that we are all connected, and are all experiencing this together?

## [Awakened Circles by Lu Jun](https://artchinauk.com/awakened-circles-lu-jun/)

We are very excited to introduce you to our new artist, Chinese sculptor, Lu Jun.

He graduated from the sculpture department of Xi’an Academy of Fine Arts in 1989, and has, for more than 40 years, been engaged in painting, public art, and sculpture. He then lived in Shenzhen, China, a city that is becoming the front line for contemporary Chinese art in China. His public sculpture is easy to spot in the city.

Recently, Lu Jun moved in Cambridge, in the UK to continue his creativity. Below are two sculptures which we are going to exhibit at the Affordable Art Fair in Battersea, London. They are titled the “Awakened Circle” series which is an extension of his “BABY” series. The sculptures explore the idea of combining and deconstructing various life forms, connecting with public environments and facilities in our real social lives, as well as inspiring the senses to inspire viewers to think about the next generation and our future.

## [Art Enables Understanding of Diseases and Healing | 艺术、疾病与治愈](https://artchinauk.com/art-enables-to-understand-diseases-and-healing-%e8%89%ba%e6%9c%af%e3%80%81%e7%96%be%e7%97%85%e4%b8%8e%e6%b2%bb%e6%84%88/)

_**Originally published by [CAFA Art Info](https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/RfCGvdkEJnLISvr5i\_OLGQ)**_

人类有多惧怕疾病和死亡？个体的疾病与死亡不仅仅是人类生命体内的破坏与终结，也与生命系统的环境变化和发展有着紧密的联系。自二十世纪以来人类在创造奇迹的同时也在制造着灾难，人类社会物质财富迅猛增长，而与此同时人类对于自然和生物环境的破坏也无以复加。

How much do people fear diseases and death? An individual’s disease and death do not just mean the destruction and end of human life, but also have a close relationship with the environmental changes and development of living systems. Since the 20th century, people have been creating miracles while also bringing about disasters. The material wealth of society has grown rapidly, but meanwhile the manmade damages to the natural and biological environment also repeatedly occur.

尽管疾病伴随着人类的生活，痛苦却让我们真实地感觉活着并在某种意义上证明了我们的存在。正是在思考疾病、研究疾病、惧怕灾难和逃避死亡的探索中, 人类致力于去寻求慰籍与治愈。伴随着人类文明的发展，艺术家们敏锐地提供了各种各样表现疾病及其内涵的创作，进而警示人类行为并探讨人类治愈这样的普世主题。

Although diseases have always accompanied human life, pain makes us feel alive and, in a sense, proves our existence. It is through the exploration of thinking about diseases, studying diseases, and fearing disasters while avoiding death that people are committed to seeking comfort and healing. Along with the development of human civilisation, artists have keenly provided a variety of creations portraying diseases and their connotations, and further give us a profound warning regarding human behaviour while exploring such a universal topic as healing.

![Image 145](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/02/Screenshot-2020-02-24-at-15.22.06.png)**Images:**_1985年11月15日 纽约市政厅附近的示威游行者抗议市政厅考虑立法禁止携带艾滋病毒的师生进入公立学校。Demonstrators protest near New York City’s City Hall on Nov. 15, 1985, as City Council committee considered legislation to bar students and teachers with the AIDS virus from public schools. IMAGE: APAP PHOTO/RICK MAIMA, Source: https://mashable.com/2016/10/26/aids-epidemic-study/_

谈到疾病对当代艺术的影响，艾滋病危机是无法回避的话题。二十世纪七十年代艾滋病（AIDS）从加勒比海地区（Caribbean）传入美国纽约并在其后的十年间就带走了几十万生命。理查德·彭斯，曾在1986年至2009年之间担任美国纽约LGBT团体中心负责人（Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual & Transgender), 他在Mashable于2016年进行的相关报道中[1]，表示二十世纪八十年代的纽约感觉像是处于战区，“你会感觉那时的生活伴随着恐惧、不断的死亡、彼此看护、还有战斗疲劳症”。

When it comes to the impact of diseases on contemporary art, the AIDS crisis is an unavoidable topic. In the decade after AIDS “jumped” from the Caribbean to New York City in 1970 or 1971, hundreds of thousands of US lives were taken by the disease of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Richard Burns, who was the Executive Director of the New York City LGBT Community Center from 1986 through 2009, told _Mashable_ that New York City in the 1980s felt like a war zone: “you were living with fear and constant dying and caregiving and shellshock.”

早在卫生机构认识到艾滋病危机之前，艺术家们就开始引发人们对这一问题的关注。在二十世纪八十年代的文化背景下，有关艾滋病这一有争议性的主题也在艺术圈内引发了广泛的讨论并成为艺术家为少数群体争取同等权益的触发点，从此人们逐渐意识到：艺术也可以参与社会问题的对话，并且产生不可小觑的影响力。

Even before health institutions recognised the AIDS crisis, artists started drawing attention to the issue. Art that started to concentrate on this controversial theme emerged from a broader cultural community in the 1980s. The questions about AIDS opened significant debates and they later triggered activities to fight for equal rights of minorities. Since then, people have gradually realised that art can also participate in the dialogue of social issues, and they further exert some significant influence.

![Image 146](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/02/Screenshot-2020-02-24-at-15.23.53.png)**Image:**_妮基·桑法勒为艾滋病主题创作的艺术家手制书 , Niki de Saint Phalle –AIDS, you can’t catch it holding hands, 1987, book. Photo via artnews.com_

直到1985年美国总统里根才在公众演讲中第一次提到了“AIDS” ，由于起初公众都不了解病毒来源和传播方式，艾滋病传播的危机让许多艺术家和创作者都在不知不觉中身陷疾病，凯斯· 哈林(1958-1990)也是其中之一。疾病并没有使他消沉沮丧，他创建了凯斯· 哈林基金会并为艾滋病研究治疗和儿童福利做努力，同时继续艺术创作直至生命终结，正如他在日记中所表达的，“你所做的一切都是一种对永生的追求，因为你在创造这些你知道有不同生活的东西，它们不依赖于呼吸，所以它们的寿命比我们任何人都长，它们在某种程度上延长了你的寿命。” [2]

It was not until 1985 that US President Reagan mentioned “AIDS” in a public speech. Since the majority of public did not understand the source and transmission of the virus in the decade before that, many artists and creators had been affected by the crisis, Keith Haring (1958-1990) was one of them. Although he felt frustrated because of the disease, he did not fall into a depression; instead, he founded the Keith Haring Foundation contributing to AIDS research and therapy as well as children’s welfare. He kept working on art until the end, as he wrote in his diary, “all of the things that you make are a kind of quest for immortality. Because you’re making these things that you know they have a different kind of life. They don’t depend on breathing, so they’ll last longer than any of us will. Which is sort of an interesting idea, that it’s sort of extending your life to some degree.”

![Image 147](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/02/Screenshot-2020-02-24-at-15.25.13.png)**Images:**_凯斯· 哈林 《无视＝畏惧》(1989), Keith Haring, “Ignorance = Fear” (1989), Courtesy of the Keith Haring Foundation_

艾滋病流行所产生的社会危机感成为了二十世纪八十年代很多美国艺术家创作的主题，并且极大地改变了当代艺术世界。“愤怒、困惑、恐惧和蔑视，一切皆由艺术家的生存现状和文化的兴起所激发，既是对危机的一种回应，也很大程度上改变了主流自我反省式的艺术创作手法，使艺术更接近政治和生活。” [3]

The AIDS epidemic crisis became the topic of artworks in the 1980s by many American artists using diversified methods and transformed the world of contemporary art significantly. “Anger, confusion, fear and defiance, all triggered by the artists’ existential situation and the emergence of culture which formed a response to the crisis, having immensely changed the dominant self-reflexive art practices, bringing art closer to politics and life.”

![Image 148](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/02/Screenshot-2020-02-24-at-15.26.24.png)**Image:**_弗兰克·摩尔 《竞技场》(1992) 木板布面油彩丝网, Frank Moore, “Arena,” 1992. Oil and silkscreen on canvas mounted on wood, in antique gilded frame. 61 x 72”. Collection of Gian Enzo Sperone, Sent, Switzerland. Image: Courtesy Sperone Westwater, New York._

美国艺术家弗兰克·摩尔（1953 – 2002)在作品中描述了DNA重组、人体工程学和基因组合等等意象并表现了他所处的炼狱般现实（艾滋病感染者）和他对地狱的想象，正如他所述，“尽管我们现代的世外桃源看起来如此美丽，但这是融合了现代生活所有复杂性和毒性的美丽。”[4]

Frank Moore (1953 – 2002) portrays a brilliant parade of DNA manipulations, human engineering and genomes in his work, with which he conveyed the reality of his purgatory and his own dream of hell, on which he stated that, “as beautiful as our modern Arcadia may appear to be, it is a beauty that is alloyed with all the complexities and toxicities of modern life.”

于是当人类践踏着无可再生的资源破坏和其他动物的残骸，昂首阔步迈进21世纪的“美丽新世界”时，这“复杂性和毒性”仍在蔓延。除了人类尚未完全克服的疾病外，我们还面临着更多的威胁和挑战。

These complexities and toxicities are still spreading as humans trample on the destruction of non-renewable resources and the remains of other animals and stride into the “brave new world” in the 21st century. In addition to the diseases that human beings have not completely overcome, we are constantly confronted with more threats and challenges.

![Image 149](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/02/Screenshot-2020-02-24-at-15.28.01.png)**Image:**_埃里克·艾弗里 《新兴传染病》(2000) 石版套麻胶版画 Eric Avery, “Emerging Infectious Diseases” (2000), linoleum block print over lithograph (Department of Rare Books and Special Collections, Graphic Arts Collection, Princeton University Library © Eric Avery)_

美国普林斯顿大学美术馆近期的展览《健康的状态：设想疾病与治愈》(2019年11月2日至2020年2月2日）纵观历史和多元文化，呈现了从上古到现今关于疾病与治愈的八十余件全球性艺术作品。[5]其中埃里克·艾弗里的作品 《新兴传染病》刻画了围绕流行病和传染病的社会焦虑，生与死转瞬切换的距离，发人深醒。

The recent exhibition throughout history and across cultures, entitled _State of Health: Visualizing Illness and Healing_(November 2, 2019 through February 2, 2020) presented by the Art Museum of Princeton University, featured over 80 works of globe-spanning art. “Emerging Infectious Diseases” (2000) by Eric Avery examines the societal anxiety about pandemics and infectious disease, the instantaneous switching between life and death, which has a sobering connotation.

![Image 150](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/02/Screenshot-2020-02-24-at-15.34.46.png)**Image:**_俄罗斯艺术家宝琳娜 《屏住呼吸》 曾于2017年3月24日（世界肺结核日）在世界卫生组织日内瓦总部展出。 Russian artist Paulina Siniatkina, “Hold Your Breath”, was exhibited at the headquarters of the World Health Organization (WHO) in Geneva on 24 March 2017 （World TB Day)._

对于受疾病启发而进行创作的当代艺术家们来说，“感恩胜于痛苦”。2015年俄罗斯艺术家宝琳娜在莫斯科的结核病医院度过了6个月17天，在这个过程中她经历了恐惧、误解、愤怒、绝望、孤独、沉默、爱、友情和希望。[6]《屏住呼吸》系列作品讲述了她和遭遇相似病况其他病人的故事，也是她对抗疾病的武器并以此敦促人们不要畏惧耻于谈论结核病才能更有效地阻止疾病蔓延。

For artists who have been inspired by illness, “gratitude outweighs pain”. In 2015, Russian artist Paulina Siniakina spent six months and 17 days in a TB clinic in Moscow. She went through fear, misunderstanding, anger, despair, loneliness, silence, love, friendship, and hope. Her “Hold Your Breath” series tells stories of herself and other people who shared her fate, which she takes as a weapon to fight the stigma of disease and urges people not to be afraid to talk about TB.

美国艺术家迪伦· 莫蒂默经历了两次双肺移植手术，他曾患有囊性纤维化，疾病使得他呼吸困难而艺术成为他处理和探索疾病的方式。迪伦· 莫蒂默由肺和身体细胞的结构图形受到启发进行创作，每一件作品都承载着他痛苦的重量，但他依然很乐观地说，“我相信在最绝望的情况下仍有希望，这也当然是我还活着的原因。” [7]

American artist Dylan Mortimer has endured two double lung transplants during his life. Cystic fibrosis clogged his lungs, making him feel it is hard to breathe, but art has become a way for him to process and explore his disease. Inspired by the structure of lungs and cells of his body, he creates with their patterns and shapes, yet every piece holds the weight of his pain. He still believes that “there is hope in the most hopeless situations, that’s certainly what has kept me alive.”

![Image 151](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/02/Screenshot-2020-02-24-at-15.36.17.png)**Image:**_迪伦· 莫蒂默 《升》（2016）；右：迪伦· 莫蒂默 《带来和解的拒绝》（2019） From left: “Ascension” by Dylan Mortimer, 2016; “Rejection that Brings Reconciliation” by Dylan Mortimer, 2019(COURTESY OF DYLAN MORTIMER)_

除了从自身的经历出发，还有更多的国际艺术家从科学和医学的视角，探索并质疑人类与细菌、病毒和传染病的关联，以及生物学研究和新科技的干预。

In addition to starting from their own experiences, there are more international artists using scientific and medical perspectives, exploring and questioning the relationship between humankind to bacteria, viruses, and infectious diseases, as well as the interventions of biological research and new technologies.

![Image 152](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/02/Screenshot-2020-02-24-at-15.38.19.png)**Photo:**_玛拉·哈瑟汀《抑制非典》(2006) “SARS Inhibited” Materials: bronze, paint, rocks. Dimensions: 30′ wide, 9′ tall ©Mara G. Haseltine_

新加坡的启奥生物医药园中Epi-Center前永久矗立着由玛拉·哈瑟汀设计的雕塑作品《抑制非典》（2006）。这件室外雕塑为纪念在启奥生物医药园工作的国际科研团队发现SARS蛋白酶抑制剂而特别制作。非典SARS事件是指向于2002年在中国广东发生至2003年中期在中国北京逐渐被消灭的传染病疫潮。这件雕塑作品以拟态的形式生动地在艺术表达中结合生物科技概念，使治愈的希望与周围环境自然融合。

A bronze sculpture entitled “SARS Inhibited” (2006) by Mara G. Haseltine permanently stands in front of the Epi-Center of Biopolis in Singapore. This outdoor sculpture was created to memorise the functions of the SARS Protease Inhibitor discovered by the international team of scientists working at Biopolis. In a mimetic form, it vividly integrates biotechnology with artistic expression, hope of healing with surrounding environment.

![Image 153](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/02/Screenshot-2020-02-24-at-15.39.32.png)**Photo:**_安娜·杜米特和亚力克斯·梅 《古菌机器人：以个后奇点与后气候变化生命》(2018) ArchaeaBot by Anna Dumitriu and Alex May, Photo credit Vanessa Graf at Ars Electronica 2018 Source: http://digicult.it/articles/an-engagement-with-bacteria-interview-with-anna-dumitriu/._

英国牛津大学现代化医学微生物学项目的驻地艺术家，英国艺术家安娜·杜米特的创作涵盖雕塑、装置、织物和生物学创作, 在作品《古菌机器人：以个后奇点与后气候变化生命》（ArchaeaBot: A Post Singularity and Post Climate Change Life-form)中安娜·杜米特和亚力克斯·梅以幽默诙谐的方式想象和创作人类对抗未来灾难性炎热环境效应的方式。[8]

As an artist-in-residence with the Modernizing Medical Microbiology Project at the University of Oxford, Anna Dumitriu’s creations span sculpture, installation, textiles, and biological work. With “ArchaeaBot: A Post Singularity and Post Climate Change Life-form,” Anna Dumitriu and Alex May imagine and prepare humans for a way of living to battle the catastrophically scorching umwelt.

![Image 154](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/02/Screenshot-2020-02-24-at-15.40.47.png)**Photo:**_玛格丽塔·佩弗 《互联系统的剖析》(2017)“Anatomy of an Interconnected System” (2017). Performative lecture (Media: animal bones, blackboard, chalk, soil, cotton cloth, animal blood, caput mortum pigment. Duration: 2 h 30′). Source: www.margheritapevere.com_

着眼于当今环境危机中人与自然的复杂联系，《互联系统的剖析》 是欧洲艺术家玛格丽塔·佩弗在2017年进行的行为艺术讲座，该项目由柏林艺术实验室委托，并在柏林参议院文化和欧洲部的支持下得以实现。该艺术项目致力于讨论高科技时代中，涉及生物体和技术的艺术实践探讨人类与生物圈的相互关联性。Focusing on the complicated relationship between human and nature in context of current environmental crisis, “Anatomy of an Interconnected System” (2017) is a performative lecture conducted by Margherita Pevere. It was commissioned by Art Laboratory Berlin and realised with the support of the Berlin Senate Department for Culture and Europe. It contributes to the discussions on how artistic practices that involve living organisms and technology explore the interconnection between humans and the biosphere in this high-tech age.
从人类的健康与生存，再到人类与环境的共存与治愈，生物科技的参与和干预，艺术不仅为人类提供了丰富多样的阐释，还提出了更多的可能与设想。疾病并不可怕，可怕的是缺乏勇气与想象力。无论是身体还是心灵的治愈，无论是弱势群体的权益还是整个人类和地球的未来，皆因艺术的参与而获得更加深刻的理解并唤起更多的关注和反思。

From the health and survival of human beings to the coexistence and healing of human beings and the environment, the participation and intervention of biotechnology, art does not only provide rich and diverse interpretations for people but it also proposes more possibilities and suggestions. Diseases are not that terrible; what’s more terrible is that one lacks courage and imagination. This is true whether it is for the rights of vulnerable groups or the future of the entire human race, even the earth, all of which have gained a deeper understanding and evoked more attention and reflection due to the participation of artists.

## [More Art for the People of Wuhan, China](https://artchinauk.com/more-art-for-the-people-of-wuhan-china/)

February 10 was the first day back to work in many places outside of Hubei, China. At least hundreds of millions of people have either started working from home or walked into factories or offices wearing masks. It’s a tough choice, and all of us can only choose the relative balance between health and life. On the first day back to work, still hundreds of millions of people are also absent; it is the most profound collective practice for the Chinese people. A new case of pneumonia in Wuhan has turned into a disaster. It is close to all of our hearts and has made this Spring Festival holiday feel especially long.

In the book _The Wandering Earth_ author Liu Cixin wrote: “At first, no one cared. It was nothing more than a mountain fire, a drought, the extinction of a species, the disappearance of a city. Until this disaster touches everyone.”

A question posed online to the Chinese people: “How did you feel on the first day returning to work with this ongoing coronavirus epidemic?”

The most poignant answer was: “There has never been a time, like now, when I have felt I had been too perfunctory in my life. In the future I will work hard to earn money, work, and live seriously.”

**Yes, only when the world is quiet, can you hear your own heartbeat.**

Only through life or death and sudden changes can you realise the truth of life.

After almost 20 days at home, when the day is suddenly paused, will made you understand life more than ever.

From today on, at least hundreds of millions of people who have not lived seriously before are destined to “disappear” or “missing”.

And you, what is your biggest feeling?

**The coronavirus epidemic has not only changed the way society functions; it has changed everyone’s attitude toward the world.**

If we say the disaster is inevitable, well, the past 20 days or so have shown the most profound collective practice from the Chinese people.

The artworks below were created by ArtChina artists Yang Qi, Tang Chenghua, and Hou Weiguo in reaction to the epidemic:

![Image 156](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/02/Screenshot-2020-02-17-at-14.05.04.png)**Image:**_“Spring is coming”,oil on canvas, 80cm x200cm, by Tang Chenghua_

![Image 157](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/02/Screenshot-2020-02-17-at-14.06.37.png)**Image:**_“We are all One”, print by Hou Weiguo_

## [Art for Wuhan, China: He Kun’s Journal](https://artchinauk.com/art-for-wuhan-china-he-kun/)

This week, our blog will show a watercolour painting diary series by one of our Chinese artists, He Kun. He started this series from the first day of Chinese year with the intention of recording how did the coronavirus has impacted our daily lives especially during this special period of time that is the new year for every family in China in 2020.

![Image 158](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/02/Screenshot-2020-02-10-at-21.43.10.png)

This painting above was created on the first day of the Chinese New Year. It is titled “Wish Happy New Year”.

The setting is the Yunnan province, located in Southern China, where warm weather and brightly coloured plants bloom throughout the entire year. In this painting, t he plum tree blossoms with beautiful pink flowers in the background. You can imagine birds chipping, jumping on the ground, signifying that spring is here. But in the middle, two men wear masks, glasses, hats, and long coats; they remain distanced from one another but great each other hello with their hands.

Usually we will shake hands, and pat each other’s backs as a greeting, wishing one another a good year ahead, and we exchange gifts.

On the second day, He Kun painted “Go out for a walk”, shown below.

![Image 159](https://artchinauk.com/artchina/uploads/2020/02/Screenshot-2020-02-10-at-21.49.51.png)

Now, it is not as simple as before to go out for a walk with your do. Before, you only needed to put on the collar and lead, and off you go. But now, you need to cover yourself from head to toe, just like the person depicted in He Kun’s image. Normally, this park would be such a relaxing place to take a dog for a walk, and now that has become a dangerous task. You can’t even dare to take a deep breath outside without wearing a mask! Flowers are still blooming, birds are still singing, the sun is still shining, but you can’t enjoy it; there is no relaxing outdoors as the outbreak of the coronavirus has changed every single aspect of our daily lives.

How can this have happened to us? Why? Where did the coronavirus come from? When did the coronavirus start to spread to humans? How long is this going to last? How many people will die from this sudden tragedy before it’s under control? These are the questions people in China who are suffering are asking, and others around the world too.

**If you have created artwork relating to the impact of the coronavirus on China or the wider world, please contact us; we would love to share your work.**

## [Art for Wuhan, China](https://artchinauk.com/art-for-we-han-china/)

Yesterday, I wrote a letter to our artists on the behalf of ArtChinaUK. The response was overwhelming.

Below is the letter and some of the responses from the artists. I hope, through the art we are sharing, we will bring hope, compassion and love to everyone, especially the people of Wuhan.

“Dear artist friends,

I sincerely wish you good health and that your families are safe and sound during the current outbreak of the new coronavirus.

Through the centuries, artists have been driven by suffering, and hardship inspired the creation of many important works, such as Giovanni’s “The Decameron ” or Picasso’s “Guernica”.

Now, artists are standing with the people of Wuhan, and our hearts go out to those who are struggling with the coronavirus, whether physically or sadly watching family or friends suffering, and to those who are struggling to contain or cure the virus or invent a vaccination.

The sudden outbreak of the disease has not only plunged the Chinese people into panic and suffering, but has also alarmed the world.

At this critical time, ArtChina hopes to collect all artworks, including photos and videos, reflecting this moment in our history. We will organise and publish these pieces as a series of reports on our website and our relevant social media platforms.

We hope to connect the hearts of all mankind, bring attention to what is happening, and reflect and think critically together through your artworks.

I hope to see your work soon. Thank you very much!”

Yan Qi, a Chinese artist who lives in Dusseldorf, Germany, said, “I communicate with China every day and crave good news. I paint the most romantic pictures every day to comfort my restless heart! I hope China gets out of the epidemic soon. Chinese people will be in peace and happiness in the New Year.”

# [Exhibition Review: Aubrey Beardsley at Tate Britain](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2020/08/26/exhibition-review-aubrey-beardsley-at-tate-britain/)

*   Uncategorized
*   [Leave a comment](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2020/08/26/exhibition-review-aubrey-beardsley-at-tate-britain/#respond)

This exhibition review was first posted on the blog page for the Aubrey Beardsley Society. You can find that original post [here](https://ab2020.org/exhibition-review-aubrey-beardsley-at-tate-britain/).

✚

I must start this review with a disclaimer regarding my academic background, which may explain the approach that I take to Aubrey Beardsley’s oeuvre and the recently re-opened Tate Britain exhibition. I am an art historian, but I specialize in medical and surgical art, with a particular personal interest in anything considered ‘morbid’. Therefore, when entering the Tate, I found myself drawn to the elements of this show that dealt with illness and all themes and images that were grotesque, taboo, and decaying. Perhaps this focus also had something to do with the fact that this was my first visit to a museum since lockdown had lifted and, as with many of us, illness has been at the forefront of my mind for several months.

![Image 2: Beardsley Photo](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/beardsley-photo.jpg?w=306&h=437)

Frederick Henry Evans,_Aubrey Beardsley_, platinum print, 1894, NPG P115 © National Portrait Gallery, London

As someone working within the medical humanities, before visiting this show I was most familiar with stories and images of Beardsley’s gaunt, lithe, tuberculosis-stricken body, and with the mythologising of his illness and untimely death at age twenty-five. His death is often romanticised, as his story suits the dramatic tragedy of a typical male ‘great artist’ narrative. But, as befits the reputation and image of someone as revered today within the queer community as Aubrey Beardsley, depictions and descriptions of his disease, tuberculosis, were entwined with feminine beauty, frustrated passion, and drooping passivity in the late Victorian period; this is a conceptualisation of the disease that I first came across in Susan Sontag’s _Illness as Metaphor_.[[1]](https://ab2020.org/exhibition-review-aubrey-beardsley-at-tate-britain/#_ftn1) Beardsley was diagnosed with tuberculosis at age seven, but, as was often the case, the symptoms only erupted years later to become the haemorrhages that eventually killed him.

![Image 3: Beardsley Child at Mother's Bed](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/beardsley-child-at-mothers-bed.jpg?w=233&h=441)

Aubrey Beardsley,_Child at Mother’s Bed_, 1892, pen and Indian ink on white wove paper, Mrs Margaret Reade, Torquay, UK

Like this languishing, latent, lustful Victorian perception of tuberculosis, this exhibition is a slow, but beautiful, burn – one that is expressed in fits and starts. Beautiful, because of the undeniable quality of Beardsley’s line and compositional eye; slow, because there were points at which it felt like this show paused and diverted away from the truly explosive narrative of Beardsley’s unusual and often grotesque artistic power. Sontag describes tuberculosis as ‘a disease of extreme contrasts,’ in which the patient ‘is wracked by coughs, then sinks back, recovers breath, breathes normally; then coughs again.’[[2]](https://ab2020.org/exhibition-review-aubrey-beardsley-at-tate-britain/#_ftn2) My response to Beardsley’s drawings in this show felt delayed at several instances, like tubercular symptoms. The most glaring point at which the excitement goes latent is in a central room of the show that displayed photographs and artistic representations of and by Beardsley’s circle. The walls of this space were painted orange – a colour that the curators may have hoped (in vain) could subconsciously drum up a thrill similar to that of the lurid and erotic yellow of the literary periodical that Beardsley illustrated, _The Yellow Book_. This room concentrated on Beardsley’s friends and family, taking the viewer out of the fantastical narrative of grotesque decadence that was being built up in previous rooms. These paintings and drawings paled in comparison to Beardsley’s own production.

In contrast, the symptoms of decadence and perversion erupt most violently and satisfyingly in an eggplant-coloured alcove (perhaps a nod to that most suggestive of emojis?!) within the show’s large final room. These three purple walls are introduced with a content warning: this space holds Beardsley’s _Lysistrata_ drawings, the most overtly sexual of his oeuvre, although sexualised details and explicit phalluses appear several times in earlier rooms in this show. The placement of this alcove fits with my loose concept of this show as tubercular, as it is just before the end that the ugly (but beautiful, as tuberculosis is historically depicted) head of disease finally rears the full extent of its nastiness. In this context, however, the nastiness is what we, as viewers, have longed for all along.

![Image 4: Beardsley Lysistrata](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/beardsley-lysistrata.jpg?w=350&h=467)

Aubrey Beardsley,_Lysistrata Defending the Acropolis_, from _The Lysistrata of Aristophanes_ (1896), ca. 1929 (printed and published). Victoria and Albert Museum, London

Returning to the colours that dominated this show, and their connections to illness, there was a subtle yellow theme throughout the exhibition. The yellow walls in the show’s second room ostensibly hint at the forthcoming exploration of _The Yellow Book_, perhaps Beardsley’s most famous contribution to British visual culture. But in addition to this, the association of points to a further connotation of the colour yellow: it can be likened to the particular hue of coughed-up sputum that suggests a lung infection diagnosis. The colour of the walls also reminds viewers of another late Victorian artistic rumination on illness and confinement: Charlotte Perkin Gilman’s _The Yellow Wallpaper._

![Image 5: Beardsley Yellow Book](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/beardsley-yellow-book.jpg?w=327&h=394)

Aubrey Beardsley, cover design for _The Yellow Book_, vol. I, 1894. The British Library, London

The last room of this exhibition suggests that the ‘sickness’ that Beardsley began during his lifetime has continued to spread and to infect millions of people around the world. One of my favourite works from this final space, _In Memoriam_(c. 1923) by an unknown artist, imagines a death-bed scene, compiled of Beardsley’s own characters – both the fashionable and the grotesque. The time-tested fixation on the taboo elements of his work, as well as his distinctive forms and lines, shows that the Beardsley disease is here to stay, with no vaccine _en route_, or, for that matter, desired.

# [Dangle ‘Ums and Marsupial Pouches: World War II Plastic Surgery Techniques and Humour](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2020/07/15/dangle-ums-and-marsupial-pouches-world-war-ii-plastic-surgery-techniques-and-humour/)

*   Uncategorized
*   [Leave a comment](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2020/07/15/dangle-ums-and-marsupial-pouches-world-war-ii-plastic-surgery-techniques-and-humour/#respond)

This post originally appeared on the Surgery & Emotion blog([link](http://www.surgeryandemotion.com/blog)). Check out the Surgery & Emotion project’s amazing publications ([link here)](http://www.surgeryandemotion.com/publications) or follow them on Twitter ([link](https://twitter.com/SurgicalEmotion)).

✚

It’s almost a cliché to acknowledge that humour is used in difficult situations to defuse tensions or to alter the mood.But in these last few months, we’ve seen a proliferation of jokes regarding the Covid-19 crisis: most frequently, through memes and tweets, such as the many humorous takes on the government’s official coronavirus advice and graphics. ([link](https://twitter.com/Cain_Unable/status/1259357834069901312))

I’ve found this interesting in the context of my research on the visual culture and humour of plastic surgery during the Second World War. Humour, in both images and words, thrived in the plastics wards. But here I’d like to focus on two particular surgical technologies that were used to treat patients with facial injuries and burns: the skin flap and the tube pedicle.

A skin flap is exactly what it sounds like: a surgically detached flap of skin that can be transferred to another area. For a tube pedicle, the skin is rolled to prevent infection, and both ends of the tube are attached to the body to ensure blood flow before one end is removed and connected to the injury so that it can be sculpted into a new nose or chin. Thousands of drawings and photographs were made during the Second World War of these surgical techniques. But there were also images of and comments on these tubes and flaps that play on their strangeness through humour.

Tube pedicles became a ubiquitous tool for facial reconstruction during the First World War. Harold Gillies remarked on them often in his 1957 book _The Principles and Art of Plastic Surgery_. As the most prominent plastic surgeon in Britain in the twentieth century, Gillies’s sense of humour contributed significantly to the culture of the field. In his typically humorous and exaggerated manner, Gillies wrote that his World War I plastic surgery ward in Sidcup ‘soon resembled the jungles of Burma, teeming with dangling pedicles.’[[1]](http://www.surgeryandemotion.com/blog/view/dangle-ums-and-marsupial-pouches-world-war-ii-plastic-surgery-techniques-and-humour#_ftn1) This incongruous description jars with our understanding of the tube pedicle as an invasive, uncomfortable object for the patient to whom it is attached. Gillies commented on the tube pedicle again about a hundred pages later in the book:

If all the tube pedicles that I have made and those my assistants have made were laid end to end, by calculations at two and a half pedicles per week, they would string like sausages from Buckingham Palace down the Mall, straight on through the Admiralty Arch to Trafalgar Square and half-way up Nelson’s monument. It is my ambition that before my last pedicle is made we will reach the top of this famous pinnacle with at least one pedicle left to go into the Admiral’s palate.[[2]](http://www.surgeryandemotion.com/blog/view/dangle-ums-and-marsupial-pouches-world-war-ii-plastic-surgery-techniques-and-humour#_ftn2)

Gillies’s ability to make jokes like this suggests either that he could detach himself—physically, emotionally, or temporally—from the suffering inflicted by this surgical technique, or that the humour is itself a manifestation of Gillies’s own trauma. There is also the possibility that Gillies, and other surgeons, could have utilised humour as a coercive, perhaps patronising, tactic: one that could make their patients feel like their traumas were minimal or less serious. Whatever the justification for this tone, Gillies successfully infuses the tube pedicle with humour through his animated language.

Perhaps surprisingly, facial surgery patients themselves made similar comments about their tube pedicles. Some patients gave this unsightly and uncomfortable fleshly apparatus a humorous nickname: ‘dangle ‘um.’ There was a social group in Scotland, similar to one in England (the Guinea Pig Club), that was formed around this particular trial of facial reconstruction, called The Dangle ‘Ums Club.[[3]](http://www.surgeryandemotion.com/blog/view/dangle-ums-and-marsupial-pouches-world-war-ii-plastic-surgery-techniques-and-humour#_ftn3) This language trivialises and infantilises the tube pedicle—such a light-hearted name lessens the fear of and aversion to the surgically constructed roll of flesh.

![Image 7: fs](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/fs.jpg?w=323&h=426)

Dickie Orpen, BAPRAS/DSB 7.26, pencil on paper, Archives of the British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive and Aesthetic Surgeons, London.

A similar goal is met in a drawing by the artist Dickie Orpen, who was based in St Albans at Hill End Hospital’s plastic surgery ward during the Second World War. In this image, a combination skin flap and tube pedicle is being transposed. Even though this is a highly specialised image, meant to show the numbered steps of this surgical procedure, it is also transgressive in its sense of humour. In the centre of the image, the surgical artist has ‘christened’ the roll of flesh with the name ‘Angus,’ dating it January 13th, 1943, 2:55 pm. There is room in this page, and in the surgical ward as a whole, for play and humour in the face of pain and distress.

Like Orpen, Gillies used images to imbue tube pedicles and skin flaps with humour. Gillies’s 1957 book is incredibly odd; not only is it written in a humorous tone (evident in the tube pedicle quotations above), but the descriptions of some truly horrific facial injuries and full-body burns are often accompanied by irreverent cartoons and photographs. One reviewer called it ‘a combination of autobiography, an unorthodox text, an informal reference book, filled with the most astounding array of illustrations … as well as a complete drama in the development of plastic surgery.’[[4]](http://www.surgeryandemotion.com/blog/view/dangle-ums-and-marsupial-pouches-world-war-ii-plastic-surgery-techniques-and-humour#_ftn1)

![Image 8: Gillies, Harold, and D. Ralph Millard, Jr. The Principles and Art of Plastic Surgery, vol. 1, preface, np, 1957, published by Butterworth & Co. ](https://i0.wp.com/www.surgeryandemotion.com/content/images/Gillies_1957_Prologue.JPG)
Gillies, Harold, and D. Ralph Millard, Jr._The Principles and Art of Plastic Surgery_, vol. 1, preface, np, 1957, published by Butterworth & Co.

In the prologue, there is an image of a man with a long nose with birds perched upon it, drawn by the artist and nonsense poet Edward Lear (who happened to be Gillies’s great-uncle). The poem below it humorously states that this nose could be stolen and used as a tube pedicle. But perhaps the strangest image in this book is in the section on ‘Direct Flaps,’ on a page describing ‘The “Marsupial” Flap.’ Here, Gillies inserted a photograph of a surgeon into the ‘pouch’ that the flap makes around a real patient’s abdomen. In my research on this topic and this period, it seems that there are few lines that humour cannot cross in plastic surgery, as even an ostensibly serious publication by two established surgeons can have a visual joke like this within it.

![Image 9: Gillies, Harold, and D. Ralph Millard, Jr. The Principles and Art of Plastic Surgery, vol. 1, p. 151, 1957, published by Butterworth & Co. [full page and detail as featured image] ](https://i0.wp.com/www.surgeryandemotion.com/content/images/Gillies_1957_Marsupial_Flap_2.JPG)
Gillies, Harold, and D. Ralph Millard, Jr._The Principles and Art of Plastic Surgery_, vol. 1, p. 151, 1957, published by Butterworth & Co. [detail of this image is at the top of the page, as the Featured Image]

As I’ve alluded to above, the question of _who_ is making these visual and verbal jokes matters. There are ethical and personal differences between patients making fun of their own faces, surgical artists adding humour to the depicted procedures, and surgeons making light of their practice. Further thought and research will have to be given to these questions of coercion, agency, and humour in a longer piece of writing, but this blog post hopefully begins the conversation.

# [‘Handworkers’: Art, Surgery, and the Hands that Craft](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2020/04/14/handworkers-art-surgery-and-the-hands-that-craft/)

*   Uncategorized
*   [Leave a comment](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2020/04/14/handworkers-art-surgery-and-the-hands-that-craft/#respond)

In their book _Operative Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery_ (1980), John N. Barron and Magdy N. Saad provide a potted etymology of the word ‘surgery’:

‘The word _surgery_ in English is derived from the older word form _chirurgery_, related to the French _chirugie_ and Latin _chirurgia_… Similarly, the word _surgeon_ is related to the Greek _kheirougos_. The Greek word contains two roots; _khier_, a hand and _ergon_, which means work or activity… In effect therefore, surgery means handworking and a surgeon is a handworker. Although the word _kheirourgos_ could indicate any handworker, its use has been largely restricted to the medical sense for some 2000 years, as have all European words and derivatives.’ [[1]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn1)

The focus in Barron and Saad’s definition here is the hands-on reality of surgery. Their emphasis is on the craftmanship of the work, and, in this instance, surgery is not the cerebral, detached, scientific profession that it is sometimes cast as being. Much of the visual language surrounding surgery—particularly plastic surgery—compares the work of the surgeon to the work of the artist. This idea of being a ‘handworker’ provides a concrete, visual tie between these two occupations, and this blog post will spotlight a few fascinating examples of hands being conceived of as the focus of genius and as the key marker of the practitioner’s identity—in both of these seemingly disparate jobs.

Many surgeons are and were amateur artists in their spare time, making cartoons, sculptures, or paintings; several of the practical and linguistic elements of the field point to this fact. [[2]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn2) For example, today’s plastic surgery tools—such as those with the ‘Barron’ handle, named for the surgeon quoted above—have octagonal rather than round handles, which allow for quick, precise, and artistic rotations. [[3]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn3) Textbooks and articles on plastic surgery include ‘art’ or ‘sculpture’ in their titles as well as hand-drawn illustrations from surgical artists. [[4]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn4) Saad describes his patients as his pieces of art, worthy of being hung like a painting or placed like a sculpture in the cluttered halls of the Chelsea Arts Club. [[5]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn5) Additionally, a prominent surgeon who worked with John Barron was considered to be ‘an artist and a craftsman’ when it came to sculpting live tissue in a surgical reconstruction. [[6]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn6)

[![Image 11: Barbara Hepworth The Artist's Hand](https://i0.wp.com/morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/barbara-hepworth-the-artists-hand.png?w=395&h=246&ssl=1)](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2020/04/14/handworkers-art-surgery-and-the-hands-that-craft/barbara-hepworth-the-artists-hand/)

[![Image 12: Barbara Hepworth Hand II horizontal](https://i0.wp.com/morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/barbara-hepworth-hand-ii-horizontal.png?w=327&h=246&ssl=1)](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2020/04/14/handworkers-art-surgery-and-the-hands-that-craft/barbara-hepworth-hand-ii-horizontal/)

[Figure 1:Barbara Hepworth,_The Artist’s Hand_, 1943-4, Tate.]

[Figure 2:Barbara Hepworth,_Hand II (horizontal)_, 1950, private collection.]

The focus on the artistry and genius of the surgeon’s hand does not stop at plastic surgery. As many mid-century surgeons saw their surgery as sculpting human flesh, it is particularly fascinating to see the relationship between a renowned sculptor (Barbara Hepworth) and a well-known surgeon (Norman Capener). In 1947, Capener, an orthopedic surgeon, invited Hepworth to sketch his operations, having met her when Hepworth’s daughter had been ill. I previously wrote about Hepworth’s surgical drawings that result from these hours of observation in the blog post ‘Barbara Hepworth’s Hospital Drawings: Sculptural, Surgical, Tactile, Haptic’ from March 2018. Some of the discussion of the importance of hands in Hepworth’s surgical works can also be found there. As a sculptor who used the practice of ‘direct carving’ to create her works, Hepworth was particularly focused on the power of the artist’s hand and the scope of work that could be created with one’s hands. In a speech given to surgeons in 1953, Hepworth stated, ‘As I became more accustomed to the various operations I began to realize how profoundly important from an artist’s point of view the expression of the human hand is. Not only is it the most revealing and expressive part of the human body—it is also the visible extension of the brain and feeling generally.’ [[7]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn7) Through her work in operating theatres, Hepworth discovered the parallels of her own use of hands and touch to that of surgeons. Around 1943, Hepworth made a cast of her left hand, which she called her ‘thinking’ hand, titled _The Artist’s Hand_(Fig. 1). [[8]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn8) And after spending two years observing Capener’s surgeries, Hepworth cast a bronze sculpture of his hand entitled _Hand II (horizontal)_ (Fig. 2). By creating these similar casts, Hepworth elevated the status of the tactile skills of both surgeon and sculptor, turning the physical conduit of that skill into a work of art itself. This must have been a particularly affecting exchange for Capener, who was an amateur sculptor himself, to have his hand depicted by such a prominent sculptor. Capener’s wife donated his _Clasped Hands_(Fig. 3) sculpture to the Royal College of Surgeons in 1976. According to an article covering this donation, Capener ‘was always keenly interested in hands, in surgery, pottery, and all forms of craftsmanship’—as was his friend and collaborator, Barbara Hepworth. [[9]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn9)

![Image 13: Norman Capener Clasped Hands](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/norman-capener-clasped-hands.jpg?w=404&h=408)

[Figure 3:Norman Capener,_Clasped Hands_, c. 1951, Royal College of Surgeons.]

Images of surgeons’ hands can be used for more obviously self-serving purposes, as seen in the colour photographs that Percy Hennell took of two prominent British plastic surgeons Harold Gillies (Fig. 4) and Archibald McIndoe (Fig. 5). The striking image of Gillies’s gloved hands against a deep green background served as the cover for his 1957 book _The Principles and Art of Plastic Surgery_. Like a sculptor or a painter, Gillies gingerly and expertly holds the tools of his trade. The aesthetic, slightly asymmetrical composition that Hennell has created adds to the artistic connotations of the plastic surgeon’s professsion. The photograph of McIndoe’s hands is quite different from the one of Gillies, as it is not as static nor as precisely composed. Rather, this image of McIndoe’s hands touts the stability and confidence of the surgeon’s hands. With something as sensitive as a patient’s eye, and with a small dropper tool, McIndoe’s gloved hands are precise and sure in their movements. It is also telling that even though her eye is being opened by force by McIndoe’s gloved hand, the patient (perhaps sedated) appears calm and unworried by the surgeon’s intrusion.

[![Image 14: HEN:11:5](https://i0.wp.com/morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/hen115.jpg?w=352&h=448&ssl=1)](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2020/04/14/handworkers-art-surgery-and-the-hands-that-craft/hen115/)

[![Image 15: McIndoe's Hands Downloaded](https://i0.wp.com/morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/mcindoes-hands-downloaded.jpg?w=370&h=448&ssl=1)](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2020/04/14/handworkers-art-surgery-and-the-hands-that-craft/mcindoes-hands-downloaded/)

[Figure 4: Percy Hennell,_Harold Gillies’s Hands_, c. 1957, Archives of the British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive, and Aesthetic Surgeons, London]

[Figure 5: Percy Hennell,_Archibald McIndoe’s Hands_, Archives of the British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive, and Aesthetic Surgeons, London]

These examples of Capener’s, Gillies’s, and McIndoe’s hands show that surgeon’s hands were of interest in artistic representations. But even when the hand is not the overt focus in a piece of surgical art, it can end up being what the artist emphasizes or what viewers pick up on when observing the piece. One example is William Orpen’s portrait of the surgeon Ivor Back (Fig. 6) from 1926. The tight, dark gloves are similar to those worn by Gillies and McIndoe in their hand portraits. And yet this portrait is about the entirety of the surgeon, and is not specifically focused on his hands. But by painting most of the composition in light colors to correspond with the doctor’s surgical dress, Orpen has drawn the viewer’s eyes immediately to Back’s hands and head. In _Sir William Orpen: Artist and Man_(1932), P. G. Konody and Sidney Dark write that in this painting, the ‘form and weight of the body are felt through the white overall, although the material is far from pliant or clinging. A superb passage of expressive painting is found in the hand. Although it is covered by a brown rubber glove and shown in a limp state of complete relaxation, it is unmistakably a capable hand, firm and sensitive and dependable in the professional use of the scalpel.’ [[10]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn10) Much of these descriptors could also be applied to either of the gloved hands in Hennell’s photographs.

![Image 16: Orpen The Surgeon Ivor Back](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/orpen-the-surgeon-ivor-back.jpg?w=730)

[Figure 6:William Orpen,_The Surgeon (Ivor Back)_, 1926, The Hunterian Museum at the Royal College of Surgeons]

Moving on from surgeons, there are many examples of artists’ hands being the focuses of visual works or being thought of as the nexus from which genius springs. But there is an interesting example of William Orpen’s hand—the hand that emphasized the quiet strength and skillful pliability of a surgeon’s hand—being lauded and studied as the most important part of the artist’s body. Noel Jacquin, a leading figure in British palmistry during the twentieth century, christened Orpen’s hand as ‘a perfect example of the artistic hand.’ [[11]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn11) Jacquin had several reasons for why Orpen’s hand contained artistic genius, quoting attributes like ‘conical finger tips’ as the elements that held the key to Orpen’s skill. While palmistry is a disproved pseudoscience, the twentieth-century fascination with the hand of the artist, and the hand of the surgeon, remains. It is understandable for people to see a kernel of intrinsic talent living within these fingertips, bones, and muscles. Of course, at the very base of it, art historian Mary Hunter sums up the practical side of it best: ‘Both surgical and artistic practice requires a connection of mental and manual ability and expert hand-eye coordination; drawing, painting, sculpting, and performing surgery are all visual and haptic activities that utilize similar specialized knowledge.’ [[12]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn12) Hunter’s chapter ‘Art and Surgery: The Expert Hands of Artists and Surgeons’ in the _Palgrave Handbook of the History of Surgery_(2018) is an excellent source to read for a more in-depth look at the theoretical implications of the parallels between artists’ and surgeons’ hands.

# [Joseph Maclise’s Surgical Anatomy: Face and Fiction](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2019/12/06/joseph-maclises-surgical-anatomy-face-and-fiction/)

*   Uncategorized
*   [3 Comments](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2019/12/06/joseph-maclises-surgical-anatomy-face-and-fiction/#comments)

Joseph Maclise (1815-1880) was a British anatomist and artist. His works, such as _Comparative Osteology_(1847), _Surgical Anatomy_(1851), and _On Dislocations and Fractures_(1859) contain beautiful images of anatomy as it applied to surgery. But these are not the anatomical illustrations that we are used to today (clinical and objective). Maclise’s work was influenced by the artistic and scientific trends of his day and therefore his surgically dissected figures are Classically-inspired. This blog post will focus on _Surgical_ _Anatomy_,and particularly on the faces of the corpses depicted within this publication.

The faces of these anatomical subjects are often the most attention-grabbing elements of these compositions. The expressions range from zombie-like or despondent to dramatic and noble. Not all of Maclise’s faces in _Surgical Anatomy_ are theatrical, but even when the eyes are closed often the face has a bright complexion and an alert pose. To me, one of the most striking aspects of Maclise’s work is the tension between the obvious morbidity of the subject and the animated, expressive face. This is particularly interesting because this publication emphasizes, even just in its title, that it is intended for surgeons; historian of visual communications Kim Sawchuk has pointed out that the living body is a much more useful point of study for trainee surgeons than the corpse.[[1]](https://97bdeebf-788c-4ed6-93b7-4acfcdb9d338/#_ftn1) Maclise tries to bridge this gap of knowledge in the introduction to his second edition(published 1856): he states that he and his team ‘dissect the dead body in order to furnish the memory with as clear an account of structures of its living representative, as if this latter, which we are not allowed to analyze, were perfectly translucent, and directly demonstrative of its component parts.’[[2]](https://fcc49d60-a4db-4a76-a8dc-e0ea9504ad72/#_ftn1)Perhaps this is why Maclise animates his bodies–to thinly maintain an illusion that these corpses are like the living bodies that the surgeons looking at _Surgical Anatomy_ will be operating on in the future.

![Image 18: Maclise Belvedere Torso example.png](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/maclise-belvedere-torso-example.png?w=507&h=274)

[Figure 1:_Belvedere Torso_, c. 2nd century BC, Vatican Museum AND Andreas Vesalius, from _De humani corporals fabrica_, 1543.]

Maclise’s figures, despite their animated or lively faces, lack a strong human connection between viewer and subject because of their idealized, Classicized bodies. This tradition of enlivening anatomical figures that are clearly deceased goes back to Vesalius’s sixteenth-century _Fabrica_, which uses Classical art, such as the Belvedere Torso (Fig. 1), as the basis for some of its illustrations of dissected bodies. Maclise carries on in this history of anatomical illustration with his attractive subjects, and he adds the vivid facial expressions that were often also present in Classical statuary. As Cindy Stemackowich described in her 2008 article ‘Bodies of Knowledge,’ nineteenth-century anatomical artists like Maclise had the uncanny tendency to breathe life into their images of dissected corpses. This artificial liveliness is achieved through tense musculature, warm skin tones, and well-groomed hair.[[3]](https://debfe0e9-6ad5-4820-81c8-3e6eb1c6ff3d/#_ftn1)For example, Plate VIII (Fig. 2) in the second edition of Maclise’s _Surgical Anatomy_ shows a man looking into the distance. Maclise’s figure also has his mouth partially open, so he could be seen to be inhaling or exhaling, and the deep indentation between his collarbone and trapezius muscle also suggests this action. This subject tenses his muscles and looks away from the site of medical entry, as one might do while getting an injection at the doctor’s office today. The expression is not as dramatic as some of Maclise’s others, but he certainly does not look like a cadaver; there is an effort by Maclise to create some sort of internal reaction made external–to make this man look alive.

![Image 19: IMG_9961](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/img_9961.jpg?w=730)

[Figure 2: Joseph Maclise, Plate VIII in _Surgical Anatomy_ 2nd ed., 1856]

However, the illusion is shattered by the string holding his right arm–a ‘mark of truth’ in the words of William Hunter and elaborated upon by Martin Kemp.[[4]](https://c7cb89f8-34d1-48b3-b36d-c6142d94b252/#_ftn1) While this face is one of Classicized artifice and idealized masculine pulchritude, the string locates us in the dissecting room. The same can be said for the image of the male and female corpses at the top of this blog post. Viewers of these images would have been familiar with the lively (and obviously beautified) corpses that populated the great anatomical atlases of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. As in many of those older examples, we may interpret the movements and positions of Maclise’s figures to represent breathing, or even speaking, likeness, but we cannot deny the mortality evidenced by the dissection string and the swathes of eviscerated flesh.

In comparison, there could be two interpretations of Plate IX from _Surgical Anatomy_(Fig. 3). This subject does not hold his head up and gaze away. Rather, the head lolls back. It could be depicted this way because of the simple fact that this is a corpse whose heavy head would succumb to gravity. But this body’s dead passivity could also be read as activity, as a man tensing his chest, shoulder, and neck muscles to throw his head back, roll his eyes upward, and let out a grunt or a howl. This suggests drama and emotion to the viewer, as well as feeling–as if this were a living person who still had the ability to feel. But once again, the emotion that we can read in this facial expression is braided in with the obvious visual hints and implications of this being an idealized dead person, placing a block on any real identification with the subject.

![Image 20: IMG_9964](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/img_9964.jpg?w=730)

[Figure 3: Joseph Maclise, Plate IX in _Surgical Anatomy_ 2nd ed., 1856]

There are some surgical illustrations from the twentieth century–by Henry Tonks and Dickie Orpen, who have been discussed in earlier blog posts–that allow for an identification with the patient as a real human being. This is without the constructed drama that is included in Maclise’s imagery. Even though often theatrical, we do not have an emotional reaction or a connection to the Maclise figures, as the artifice of the Victorian anatomy is evident, and this subject–or, the person who this subject once was–was dead before Maclise started to incise. Maclise could do whatever he wanted in his depictions of his corpses–who were often those from lower classes or those somehow looked down upon by society. Within Maclise’s images, these are specimens, not people, no matter what the facial expressions try to convey.

# [The Drugged Dames of the Fin-de-Siècle](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2019/10/04/the-drugged-dames-of-the-fin-de-siecle/)

*   Uncategorized
*   [Leave a comment](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2019/10/04/the-drugged-dames-of-the-fin-de-siecle/#respond)

During the Third Republic (1870-1940), France’s unstable geopolitical status bred in its people a deep uncertainty and fear of weakening agents such as venereal disease, alcoholism, and breaches of gender or social order.[[1]](https://b29ada8d-e7ca-41f4-bf7c-bc48241262c4/#_ftn1)The term _dégénérescence_ arose to describe the French national “disease” of decay on three fronts: the physical, the moral, and the intellectual.[[2]](https://b29ada8d-e7ca-41f4-bf7c-bc48241262c4/#_ftn2) During the last third of the nineteenth century, Paris was the center of the leisure industry in Europe, but morally suspect side effects accompanied this moniker.[[3]](https://b29ada8d-e7ca-41f4-bf7c-bc48241262c4/#_ftn3) The sale, use, and abuse of both women and drugs could be considered common “leisure” activities in this society. Because prostitutes were so prevalent in _fin-de-siècle_ cafés and on _fin-de-siècle_ boulevards, their image became an obsession within French art of the period, while the male clients remained largely invisible.[[4]](https://b29ada8d-e7ca-41f4-bf7c-bc48241262c4/#_ftn4) Although depicted less frequently, drugs such as morphine also became an artistic subject. Women with their addictive drugs appeared in visual art, contrasting greatly with the other typical artistic portrayals of women as idealized bastions of purity. The prints of Eugène Grasset (1845-1917) and Paul-Albert Besnard (1849-1934) exemplify this dichotomy, balancing depictions of the ideal French woman with images of the corrupted one.

![Image 22: Drugs Morphinomaniac](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/drugs-morphinomaniac.jpg?w=351&h=462)

[Figure 1: Eugène Grasset, _Morphinomaniac_, 1897, color lithograph, 41.3 x 31.4 cm, Philadelphia Museum of Art]

Morphine, originally a pharmaceutical, became a popular drug for prostitutes and other members of French society. Morphine is an opiate, meaning that it derives from opium, an extract from the poppy species _Papaver somniferum_.[[5]](https://b29ada8d-e7ca-41f4-bf7c-bc48241262c4/#_ftn5)The experience of injecting opiates includes a rush of pleasure followed by a dream-like state with reduced sensitivity or pain. As evidenced by the opiate crisis currently gripping the United States, the drugs are highly addictive, and people are drawn back into use of the drug sometimes after just one use. Symbolically, the use of morphine dovetailed in the _fin-de-siècle_ with the prostitute figure, since the rush that came with the injection has been compared to a sexual orgasm.[[6]](https://b29ada8d-e7ca-41f4-bf7c-bc48241262c4/#_ftn6)

Prints were the perfect art from with which to spread the fearsome images of seductive and drug-riddled _femmes_. Prints in the late nineteenth century were the most common and popular artistic medium.[[7]](https://b29ada8d-e7ca-41f4-bf7c-bc48241262c4/#_ftn7) They could be mass-produced and viewed by a much larger audience than a single panel or canvas painting. There was an open market in Paris for prints, and they were much more affordable and available to diverse socioeconomic classes. Because of this open market, artists had more freedom from convention than when they were making more expensive artworks that were controlled either by wealthy patrons or the French Academy.[[8]](https://b29ada8d-e7ca-41f4-bf7c-bc48241262c4/#_ftn8) While the Academy would have frowned upon Grasset’s _Morphinomania_[Fig. 1] or Besnard’s _Morphine Addicts_[Fig. 2], these were accepted in the more casual print medium.

![Image 23: Drugs Morphine Addicts](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/drugs-morphine-addicts.jpg?w=634&h=411)

[Figure 2: Paul-Albert Besnard, _Morphine Addicts_, 1887, etching, 23.7 x 37 cm, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York]

Possibly the most shocking representation of one of these drugged women appears in Grasset’s color lithograph _Morphinomaniac_, created in 1897. Grasset depicts a prostitute with flowing dark hair feeling both pain and ecstasy with the first pinch of the morphine needle in her thigh. There is great tension in her body—as there would be in an orgasm—that can be seen in between her eyebrows, in her hunched shoulders, in her clenched jaw, and in the tight grip held on her upper thigh. Sickly green and yellow forms the backdrop, supporting the idea that both promiscuity and addiction were part of the “disease” of society at the time. Dirty-looking spots emanate from the base of the composition, as if they are about to spread like an illness and engulf the woman. The sickly colors and visual allusions in this print echo the intense fear of the “venereal peril” of syphilis in Paris (see a discussion of this syphilophobia in Britain in the previous blog post) in the last decade of the nineteenth century.[[9]](https://b29ada8d-e7ca-41f4-bf7c-bc48241262c4/#_ftn9) The sex and needles utilized by women like the _Morphinomaniac_ could spread this frightening disease.

Grasset’s aesthetic choices supported late nineteenth-century French society’s prejudices against sexually promiscuous and / or drug-addicted women. Her skin is ghastly pale with an olive hue; it contrasts starkly with the prostitute’s dark stocking and with the pure white dressing gown that drapes her body. Compared to this item of clothing, she looks pallid, flat, and lifeless. The literature and art of the period reflected a strong symbolic connection between the prostitute and the corpse. The corpse obviously serves as a symbol of death, but the prostitute’s body did as well, since it was conceived as a cesspool of diseases and sin that could cause death upon contact. The procuring of cadavers for scientific or sadistic purposes occurred in the same clandestine alleys and buildings in which one procured a prostitute, furthering the negative correlation between the two figures.[[10]](https://b29ada8d-e7ca-41f4-bf7c-bc48241262c4/#_ftn10)

The _Morphinomaniac_ is also an example of the _petroleuse_, a revolting and fierce yet sexually irresistible figure.[[11]](https://b29ada8d-e7ca-41f4-bf7c-bc48241262c4/#_ftn11) The viewer of Grasset’s lithograph feels a squeamish, visceral reaction to the intense penetration of the skin on the woman’s thigh. The needle is lost deep within her flesh—itself a sexual image. Her facial expression is fierce, a descriptor of the _petroleuse_. She bares her teeth in pain, yet this expression could also be orgiastic, violent, angry, or animalistic. This image would have been a frightening one to many people in turn-of-the-century Paris. The instability and danger of injection—the riskiest method of taking morphine—is transferred to the unstable and dangerous persona of the _Morphinomaniac_. This woman is an ultimate symbol for the _petroleuse_ or the _fille publique_, and using the words of the historian Alain Corbin,this type of woman could be a “symbolic synthesis of the tragedy of the times” for the people dismayed with the _dégénérescence_ of their society.[[12]](https://b29ada8d-e7ca-41f4-bf7c-bc48241262c4/#_ftn12)

![Image 24: Drugs Spring](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/drugs-spring.jpg?w=271&h=409)

[Figure 3: Eugène Grasset, _Woman Writing_, 1892, lithograph, 121.8 x 80.8 cm, Museum of Modern Art, New York]

Compare the female type of _Morphinomaniac_ to the women in one of Grasset’s other lithographs: _Woman Writing_(Fig. 3). The action of drug taking and the emotion on the morphine addict’s face deviates markedly from the calm and idealized trope of femininity seen in this print. In _Woman Writing_, Grasset associates his female subject with objects of high learning and culture: a harp, paper, and quills. These are the items that a woman was _supposed_ to surround herself with—not bottles of morphine. This is a very different view of womankind from the cold, flat, and sickly portrayal of Grasset’s morphine addict.

The oeuvre of Grasset’s contemporary Paul-Albert Besnard further exemplifies the dichotomy between these two types of women in Parisian society, and shows the importance of the print medium in disseminating images of the more unsavory female characters. Besnard’s etched prints of the 1880s like _Morphine Addicts_ showed his marginalized subjects in unsettling ways. The figures that Besnard preferred in his prints deviated from the flattering paintings of socialites and rich courtesans for which the artist was known.[[13]](https://b29ada8d-e7ca-41f4-bf7c-bc48241262c4/#_ftn13) Besnard’s two etchings _Morphine Addicts_ and _The Cup of Tea_(Fig. 4), like Grasset’s works, clearly exhibit the two camps into which women could be placed—although _The Cup of Tea_ has a more ominous tone than Grasset’s _Woman Writing_.

![Image 25: Drugs The Cup of Tea](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/10/drugs-the-cup-of-tea.jpg?w=494&h=357)

[Figure 4: Paul-Albert Besnard, _The Cup of Tea_, 1883, etching with aquatint and drypoint, 32.5 x 25.6 cm, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York]

_Morphine Addicts_, while not explicitly portraying prostitutes, symbolizes the _femme fatale_ identity in the two depicted women. One holds a morphine quill as if offering it to the audience, reminiscent of the infamous apple offered by the first _femme fatale_, Eve.[[14]](https://b29ada8d-e7ca-41f4-bf7c-bc48241262c4/#_ftn14) She looks at the viewer with a dreamily sensual yet direct expression, with unfocused eyes and a suggestively turned head and raised eyebrows. The piece might be said to have the same feeling as a lustful dream, which is fitting, since the word “morphine” derives from _Morpheus_, the Greek god of dreams.[[15]](https://b29ada8d-e7ca-41f4-bf7c-bc48241262c4/#_ftn15)

The tea in _The Cup of Tea_ serves as an appropriate contrast to the morphine in _Morphine Addicts_. These two stimulants serve as symbols to represent the women who ingest them. The “bad” girls of _fin-de-siècle_ France take morphine, while the “good” ones, conforming to the gender roles required of them by their society, drink tea. Unlike thoroughly corrupting and addicting drugs like morphine, tea was believed to have positive health effects. Having less caffeine (technically a drug) than a cup of coffee, tea encourages cardiac health and reduces stress.[[16]](https://b29ada8d-e7ca-41f4-bf7c-bc48241262c4/#_ftn16) Tea is often associated with high society and with genteel, ladylike behavior, very different from the sensuous danger suggested by the women in _Morphine Addicts_. Besnard uses the same murky style of etching in _The Cup of Tea_ that he does in _Morphine Addicts_, but the woman is more clearly defined from her surroundings. There are no clouds engulfing the woman, and her covered head is more starkly outlined than the bare ones of the morphine addicts. While _Morphine Addicts_ shows women fading into their background, _The Cup of Tea_ depicts a more defined and refined woman.

However, the tone of _The Cup of Tea_ differs from that of _Woman Writing_. Partially because it is monochrome, _The Cup of Tea_ feels more ominous than Grasset’s piece. With this etching, Besnard hints that perhaps there is more to this woman than her feminine idealization. What is an honorable woman doing in a grim and seemingly empty café by herself? Her facial expression casts some suspicion upon her as well. Situated in profile, the viewer can see one of her eyes, so it is clear that she is not focusing on her teacup or anything else in the scene. She distractedly holds her cup, staring out into the distance, beyond the picture plane, lost in thought.

Both the drugged and the demure women in _fin-de-siècle_ prints showed important characterizations of women in French society. Using drug imagery in popular art showed the perceived proliferation of addiction in Paris at the time. The tense, sexual, and frightening portrayals of women in relation to these drugs “betrays an uncertain and often distressed worldview” that Grasset and Besnard are echoing in their visual work.[[17]](https://b29ada8d-e7ca-41f4-bf7c-bc48241262c4/#_ftn17) These images and the amoral female identity that they depict contrast greatly with the artists’ other prints that show women as either paragons of grace and intellect or as upright and proper tea drinkers.
