# [Telling Stories about Syphilis: Dr. Anne Hanley’s Arts Week Talk](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2019/05/22/telling-stories-about-syphilis-dr-anne-hanleys-arts-week-talk/)

*   Uncategorized
*   [Leave a comment](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2019/05/22/telling-stories-about-syphilis-dr-anne-hanleys-arts-week-talk/#respond)

The original version of this blog was posted on the events blog for Birkbeck, University of London ([blogs.bbk.ac.uk/events/2019/05/21/arts-week-2019-telling-stories-about-syphilis](http://blogs.bbk.ac.uk/events/2019/05/21/arts-week-2019-telling-stories-about-syphilis)). This event was part of Arts Week–an annual showcase of both scholarly and public topics by Birkbeck’s academics. The events range from lectures to exhibitions and film screenings to workshops.

![Image 27: Syphilis 1912 Richard Tennant Cooper](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/syphilis-1912-richard-tennant-cooper.jpg?w=543&h=399)

Figure 1: [Richard Tennant Cooper,_Syphilis_, 1912, Wellcome Images]

Dr. Anne Hanley began her talk this past Monday with: “Welcome everyone, to this afternoon of syphilis,” going on to give a trigger warning that if any audience member did not want to see “ulcerated genitalia,” then perhaps this paper was not for them. This arresting introduction set the tone for the entire presentation, rife with images of the ulcers that Hanley had promised but also full of thoughtful discussion on narratives of disease, widespread cultural fear, bleak Victorian literature, and propagandistic film.

The main purpose of Hanley’s paper was to trace a shift in the way that syphilis was depicted in Britain’s public imagination between the Victorian and interwar periods. Because syphilis was such a stigmatized venereal disease (VD), men and women who were infected, as well as their relatives, were more likely to suppress their stories about their experiences than to write them down or describe them in another way. Therefore, historians are often thwarted as they search for patients’ perspectives on what it was really like to experience the pustules (Figure 2), the deteriorating nasal cartilage, and even the sink into insanity associated with neurosyphilis.

![Image 28: Syphilis Face](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/syphilis-face.jpg?w=296&h=438)

Figure 2: [Franz Mracek, from his _Atlas of Syphilis and the Venereal Diseases including a brief treatise on the pathology and treatment_, 1898, Wellcome Images]

A large factor in the stigmatizing nature of the disease was that it led either to the grave or to the asylum. And this was the narrative that was espoused by Victorian authors when writing about syphilis. Hanley described how novelists used the illness as a plot point to show the medical and moral consequences of transgressing sexual mores and expectations of the time. These stories told about syphilis often followed a similar trajectory, in which a woman and her children are ruined by the moral wrongdoings of the husband. The woman, expected to be innocent and therefore ignorant of sexual matters, can become an easy victim of a morally-suspect spouse (such as the man depicted in Figure 1) and a rampant venereal disease.

This lack of knowledge was compounded at the doctor’s office once the woman sought treatment for her worrying and mysterious illness. Hanley described various medical men who used dangerous paternalism to justify keeping syphilitic women in the dark about their health. After all, the truth could result in a broken home and the damaged reputation of her husband. Often the treatment of these ill women would carry on under the pretense of a different disease, without the patient knowing the full extent of her condition. But sometimes the husbands prevented treatment from happening or from finishing for fear of the monstrous syphilitic truth coming out.

Women could stay ignorant of the risks and symptoms of venereal disease in the Victorian era because public health information was scarce. Some of the only stories that were told about syphilis were those in the plots of the novels previously described. But this double standard of men having all of the knowledge and therefore power when it came to syphilitic infection began to shift in Britain in the interwar years. The British Social Hygiene Council was established and with it came advertisements for VD clinics through posters and word of mouth but also, most importantly, films.

These cinematic visualizations of syphilis contained narratives distinct from the bleak and fatalistic ones of the Victorian-era novels. These films were often light and entertaining moral tales crafted so that viewers could identify with the characters. In one,_Any Evening After Work_(1930), a man contracts a venereal disease and considers forgoing treatment until his daughter is afflicted with the illness. While the film does use scare tactics to get people to have themselves checked at VD clinics, the overall narrative is that the little girl will get better, and everything will turn out alright–as long as the proper precautions are taken and help is sought.

This shift from pessimistic written narratives to more uplifting and informational films caused an increase of British people going to VD clinics (with both diagnosable diseases and with false alarms). Both ways of telling stories about syphilis fostered an atmosphere of syphilophobia, but the films fulfilled their propagandistic purpose of improving Britain’s sexual health and consciousness. Hanley argued that to tell stories about syphilis, we need both the fictional and the medical to understand the full cultural narrative of the disease.

# [William Orpen’s Anatomical Studies](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2019/04/17/william-orpens-anatomical-studies/)

*   Uncategorized
*   [Leave a comment](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2019/04/17/william-orpens-anatomical-studies/#respond)

William Orpen (1878-1931) is an Irish artist best known as the frontrunner of British portraiture in the Edwardian era. John Rothenstein, an art historian, director of the Tate Gallery, and Orpen’s nephew, wrote that regarding “material success [Orpen] is to be ranked, in fact, with the most successful painters who have ever worked in England—that is to say with Van Dyck, Kneller, Reynolds, Lawrence, and Sargent.”[[1]](https://59f79ac1-2ef1-4582-bbd7-8679a30c84d6/#_ftn1) In order to understand the full physicality and mortality of the stately figures who sat for his portraits, Orpen had to learn anatomy. He benefited from Henry Tonks’s style of teaching at the Slade School of Fine Art in London. Tonks was a former surgeon who advocated for the “profound study of human beings,” both physical and psychological.[[2]](https://59f79ac1-2ef1-4582-bbd7-8679a30c84d6/#_ftn2) But Orpen did not stop at learning the topic for himself and for the benefit of his own work; he taught anatomy at the Dublin Metropolitan School of Art from 1902 to 1914. Orpen’s biographer Bruce Arnold wrote how the teaching contract was irregular in these years, but by around 1906 (the approximate date for all of the anatomical drawings pictured here) Orpen was making two visits a year from London to teach in the city of his birth.[[3]](https://59f79ac1-2ef1-4582-bbd7-8679a30c84d6/#_ftn3) Continuing on the vital institutional tradition of teaching anatomy to artists (shown in the Royal Academy’s recent exhibition on the topic, _The Anatomy Professor: Doctors, Death and Dining at the RA[**[4]**](https://59f79ac1-2ef1-4582-bbd7-8679a30c84d6/#\_ftn4)_), Orpen created large-scale chalk drawings of flayed bodies at rest and in motion, labelled with letters and numbers to aid his students. Orpen had felt that his own initial artistic training at the Dublin Metropolitan School of Art in the late nineteenth century had been too focused on drawing from the Antique and not from life. He transported the anatomically-focused art at the Slade School of Fine Art to Dublin.[[5]](https://59f79ac1-2ef1-4582-bbd7-8679a30c84d6/#_ftn5)

![Image 30: Anatomical Study, Male Torso c.1906 by Sir William Orpen 1878-1931](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/william-orpen-anatomical-study-male-torso-copy.jpg?w=217&h=303)

[Sir William Orpen,_Anatomical Study, Male Torso_, c. 1906, Tate, London]

Twenty of Orpen’s anatomical works are held in the Tate Stores, near Elephant & Castle station in London. This storage complex contains the immense number of artworks not on display in one of the Tate museums or on loan to another institution. Framed and unframed works are closely filed in shelves or hung onto grated upright panels that slide in and out of the walls for easy storage. There were originally sixty known anatomical drawings by Orpen from this period, but only twenty were passed on from Orpen’s descendants to the Tate collection.[[6]](https://59f79ac1-2ef1-4582-bbd7-8679a30c84d6/#_ftn6) They have been shown in a small 2009 exhibition at Tate Britain called _William Orpen: Teaching the Body_ and in another show at Tate Liverpool called _Tracing the Century: Drawing as a Catalyst for Change_ in 2012/2013.

![Image 31: William Orpen Teaching the Body](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/william-orpen-teaching-the-body.jpg?w=730)

[Cover of the catalogue for Tate Britain’s exhibition _William Orpen: Teaching the Body_, by Robert Upstone, 2009]

The drawings are all done on thin, black paper, often on sheets that have been ripped haphazardly. Orpen was quite physical with these drawings in his classes, pinning them upon a board while lecturing. The Tate framers have put the drawings on black mounts so that these rips and irregular shapes are less noticeable, but they hint at the practical and temporary intended use of these pictures. The asymmetry of the paper on which Orpen drew is jarringly juxtaposed with the clean lines and light color of the wood frames that house these works.

![Image 32: Anatomical Study, Turning Man after Michelangelo c.1906 by Sir William Orpen 1878-1931](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/william-orpen-anatomical-study-turning-man-after-michelangelo-copy.jpg?w=231&h=375)

[Sir William Orpen, _Anatomical Study, Turning Man after Michelangelo_, c. 1906, Tate, London]

Orpen used a range of colors in his anatomical studies, but some of the works are more vibrant than others. The two images that are on the Tate’s website and used at the top of this blog post (_Anatomical Study, Male Torso_ and _Anatomical Study, Turning Man after Michelangelo_) are two of the dimmer works, but in other drawings Orpen used shocking strokes of red, pink, yellow, and blue to differentiate tendons, bones, skin, and muscle. Some of the drawings are based on famous artworks and some are more generic, but one is modeled off of Orpen’s own composition, _Nude Study_(1906). By doing this Orpen put himself into an art history lineage with the likes of Michelangelo, a lineage of artists whose work is intrinsically tied up with anatomy and the human body. He uses Michelangelo’s work as a starting point in several of these chalk drawings, but _Anatomical Study after Michelangelo_ synthesizes the flexible muscles of the figure’s écorché body with the smooth marble surface of Michelangelo’s original sculpture. Here Orpen uses Michelangelo to show how an artist can be truly successful in applying anatomical knowledge to artistic production in order to breathe life into a sculpture or drawing.

![Image 33: William Orpen Marble](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/william-orpen-marble.jpg?w=730)

[Sir William Orpen,_Anatomical Study after Michelangelo_, c. 1906, Tate, London]

The art historian Keren Rosa Hammerschlag has written convincingly on the motif of medical looking in Orpen’s work. In his teaching, “Orpen advocated that artists engage in the kind of ‘anatomical’ looking associated with medical diagnostics to penetrate the skin of their subjects to see not only the anatomy but also the psychological depth beneath.”[[7]](https://59f79ac1-2ef1-4582-bbd7-8679a30c84d6/#_ftn7) This deep piercing and perceptive gaze into the body’s flesh is visualized in Orpen’s anatomical drawings. His unflinching way of looking at skin that has been peeled away is what allowed his teaching to be effective both anatomically and artistically. Using critics during Orpen’s lifetime as her sources, Viola Barrow writes how young Orpen’s work “caused enthusiasm among the more independent critics because it was not a dead thing … but a real human figure in which every line pulsated with life.”[[8]](https://59f79ac1-2ef1-4582-bbd7-8679a30c84d6/#_ftn8) Through his chalk drawings, Orpen wanted to pass on this vigorous, medicalized vision to his own students, and Bruce Arnold emphasizes how Orpen’s teaching methods had an ‘enormous’ impact on his students and therefore the development of Irish art in the decades following Orpen’s tenure at the Dublin Metropolitan School of Art.[[9]](https://59f79ac1-2ef1-4582-bbd7-8679a30c84d6/#_ftn9)

Orpen’s focus on anatomy and medical looking becomes more interesting when one makes connections with Henry Tonks’s medical art and drawings done by William Orpen’s daughter Dickie. Tonks is perhaps best known today for his poignant portraits of facially injured servicemen from the First World War, and Dickie Orpen was employed as a surgical artist in a plastic surgery ward during World War II.[[10]](https://59f79ac1-2ef1-4582-bbd7-8679a30c84d6/#_ftn10) Henry, William, and Dickie are intertwined in their sympathetic style of examining the body and its physical interior, as well as the psychology and mortality of the individuals in their portraits (injured or not). The influence of Tonks’s teaching on William and Dickie Orpen, and William’s effect on his own students exemplifies the vital role that anatomical instruction still has on artists of the twentieth century.

# [Review of Alfred Munnings: War Artist, 1918 at the National Army Museum](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2019/02/18/review-of-alfred-munnings-war-artist-1918-at-the-national-army-museum/)

*   Uncategorized
*   [Leave a comment](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2019/02/18/review-of-alfred-munnings-war-artist-1918-at-the-national-army-museum/#respond)

As might be the case with others reading this blog post, I am familiar with Alfred Munnings (1878-1959) because of the artist’s infamous diatribe against modern art in 1949. During a dinner at the Royal Academy (of which he was the President), Munnings derided the work of modern artists like Pablo Picasso, lamenting the taste of so-called “experts” who looked down their noses at Joshua Reynolds portraits in favor of a Cubist likeness by the twentieth-century master.[[1]](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/category/uncategorized/#_ftn1)

But in addition to being a President whose envenomed speeches have not aged well (sound familiar?), Munnings was also a revered First World War artist who traveled with and painted the Canadian Expeditionary Force. As I’ve been doing research lately on William Orpen—another World War I artist—I thought that perhaps I could enjoy Munnings’s work as well. I wanted to give his paintings a chance to raise my esteem of the artist’s work and his contribution to twentieth-century art. Today I visited the National Army Museum’s exhibition of the painter’s work commissioned by Canadian War Memorials Fund in 1918. The exhibition, which is a traveling show from the Canadian War Museum, unfortunately did not succeed in redeeming Munnings for me.

![Image 35: IMG_9908](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/img_9908.jpg?w=730)

Figure 1: [Alfred Munnings,_A Grey Team, and Forest of Dreux_, 1918, oil on canvas, Beaverbrook Collection of War Art, Canadian War Museum 19710261-0474]

This shortcoming is in no way a fault of the curators of the exhibition, for it was an orderly and well-measured examination of a group of paintings that give twenty-first-century viewers an alternative view of the First World War. It seems that when it comes to World War I, the average person focuses on things like trenches and shell fire, forgetting about the thousands of horses that were used to pull lumber, charge the enemy, and carry supplies and soldiers. Munnings’s paintings express the relationship between horses and war production well, illustrating this oft-forgotten element of modern warfare. Where today’s audience might expect to see tanks and mortars, there is instead a pair of grey horses (Fig. 1) and rifles. Munnings also recorded scenes at the lumber yards that helped to fuel the war effort. Again, this is an unseen and often unrecognized labor that occurred just behind the front line; a type of work without which the soldiers would not have been able to fight and the cavalry would not have been able to charge.

![Image 36: IMG_9910](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/img_9910.jpg?w=730)

Figure 2: [Alfred Munnings,_A Stream Bed at Labergement, Jura Forest_, 1918, oil on canvas, Beaverbrook Collection of War Art, Canadian War Museum 19710261-0469]

But besides this re-conceptualization of the First World War as one run by literal horse power, any other messages from Munnings are as disparate and vague as his brushstrokes. Overall, his impressionistic paintings lack the fleeting and energizing spark of better-know French Impressionists like Monet or Degas. Munnings paints with unexpected colors as many Impressionists did. But instead of placing brushstrokes of one striking color next to another that tempers and refines it, Munnings’s colors often seem to clash with one another. For example, _A Stream Bed at Labergement, Jura Forest_(Fig. 2) uses lovely browns, greens, and greys in the rock formations in the foreground that are then ruined by the strokes of garish blue water that feels out of place with the naturalism elsewhere in the painting.

![Image 37: IMG_9933](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/img_9933.jpg?w=351&h=470)

Figure 3: [Alfred Munnings,_Brigade-Major Geoffrey Brooke, the Distinguished Service Order_ (detail), 1918, oil on canvas, Beaverbrook Collection of War Art, Canadian War Museum 19710261-0458]

When discussing a Henry Moore sculpture that he particularly despised, Munnings stated: “My horses may be all wrong—we may all be wrong—but I’m damned sure that isn’t right.” He also pleaded: “If you paint a tree—for God’s sake try and make it look like a tree, and if you paint a sky, try and make it look like a sky…”[[2]](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/category/uncategorized/#_ftn2) And yet often his own style did not reach the convincing level of naturalism that he implored other twentieth-century artists to keep at the forefront of their artistic practice. The wall text in this National Army Museum exhibition speaks of the life that Munnings’s brush breathed into his horses. However, some of the horses in the exhibition (Fig. 3) look just as lifeless as the broken down barns or ruined buildings that he also painted during the war. The horse in the above image is flattened, with seemingly arbitrary strokes of russet and dark green outlining its form. Similarly, in the piece _An April Day in the Forest_(Fig. 4), the trees that Munnings paints in the background certainly don’t look like trees—at least, they don’t look like trees from the more traditionalist aesthetic that Munnings subscribed to and promoted. These wispy translucent plants would perhaps look more at home in a Surrealist style painting, or even an illustration for a Dr. Seuss book!

![Image 38: IMG_9930](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/img_9930.jpg?w=730)

Figure 4: [Alfred Munnings,_An April Day in the Forest_, 1918, oil on canvas, Beaverbrook Collection of War Art, Canadian War Museum 19710261-0470]

There was one drawing (of which I wish there had been more) that I thought had some restorative elements (Fig. 5). The image shows a line of men on horses, stretching off into the distance. Munnings depicts the figures at the forefront in painstaking detail only to have the horses and men towards the horizon represented by simple sketched circles. This is a type of delightful abstraction (if one stretches the term) and playfulness of line that Munnings would have done well to use more often.

![Image 39: IMG_9919](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/img_9919.jpg?w=730)

Figure 5: [Alfred Munnings,_Canadian Cavalry Brigade on the March_, 1918, pencil on paper, The Munnings Art Museum 229]

In a well-put-together vitrine of the tools used to care for military horses (Fig. 6), there is a label describing how the word “dumb” was used to describe animals; there was a league called Our Dumb Friends that published a booklet to help soldiers care for their four-legged partners. This label quotes, “The term ‘dumb’ was widely used to refer to animals, because they could not speak.’” Unfortunately, Munnings’s paintings fail to speak as well. Their message is lost on a modern audience because of the saccharine nature of the scenes and the blurred depiction of a world that the viewer _wishes_ to see more clearly. Munnings’s paintings in this exhibition either give the viewer too little or too much. There are plenty of other World War I artists that visited the front and came back with affecting and substantial visual points to make about the conditions of the troops and the motivations of the countries fighting in the conflict. I think that my reaction to this Munnings exhibition is best summed up by the thoughts of a woman who passed through the Royal Academy’s Summer Exhibition in 1949, just after the President’s fateful speech against modern art. She remarked upon seeing one of his paintings, “There’s another Munnings here—dreadful. He sounded drunk the other day.”[[3]](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/category/uncategorized/#_ftn3) I appreciate the messages that the curators at the Canadian War Museum and the National Army Museum conveyed with this exhibition: that horses and lumberjacks and behind-the-front resources were just as important in the First World War as the soldiers in the trenches. It is in Munnings’s impressionistic slathering of paint on horses’ flanks and bridles that any sort of further message is lost.

![Image 40: IMG_9921](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/img_9921.jpg?w=730)

Figure 6: [Installation shot of _Alfred Munnings: War Artist, 1918_ at the National Army Museum, London, UK, 18 February 2019]

# [Psychological Trauma in an Archive of Physical Trauma](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2019/01/11/psychological-trauma-in-an-archive-of-physical-trauma/)

*   Uncategorized
*   [Leave a comment](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2019/01/11/psychological-trauma-in-an-archive-of-physical-trauma/#respond)

As an art historian working with medical drawings and photographs, I spend much of my time trawling through difficult archives filled with physically traumatic imagery. My hours spent with these collections has had a profound effect on the way that I think about how spaces can hold trauma, and how a medical archive can be structurally similar to the psychological trauma potentially endured by the patients depicted in said archive. This blog post is my way of sorting through those similarities to help explain the strong emotive, and often traumatic, effect that these archives can have on me and on other researchers.

I’ll be using one specific archive of World War II surgical material as my example: the archive of the British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive, and Aesthetic Surgeons (BAPRAS). It holds all of the known drawings made by Dickie Orpen, a medical illustrator who from 1942 to 1945 recorded plastic and reconstructive surgeries at Hill End Hospital in St. Alban’s, England. Her drawings, many of which focus on facially injured patients, are compiled either in sketchbooks or in loose sheets organized by patients’ last names. The BAPRAS archive also contains colour photographs of these patients taken by a medical photographer named Percy Hennell. These are held in plain manila folders (one for each patient) within unassuming grey boxes.

![Image 42: first hallway archive](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/first-hallway-archive.jpg?w=285&h=380)

[A view of the BAPRAS Archive, Lincoln’s Inn Fields, London, UK, photograph taken by the author]

Spending countless hours at the BAPRAS archive while researching the overlap of physical and psychological trauma in surgical art has made me realize that the structure of a traumatic archive (holding images of physical trauma) is not dissimilar from the structure of psychological trauma. A traumatic memory, which causes symptoms of psychological trauma, is one that is irrevocably fixed in the victim’s mind, long after they have survived a harmful or threatening event. Similarly, a medical archive reifies painful surgical memories by storing images of these events (ostensibly for eternity) in an institutional building, and perhaps digitally. The narratives found in the archive of Orpen’s drawings and Hennell’s photographs have become, for me, physical metaphors for various aspects, symptoms, and traits of psychological trauma. These structural metaphors have pushed me to think more critically and empathetically about the potential mental trauma from which these victims of wartime facial injury may have suffered.

✚

Flashbacks and Intrusive Memories

One of the defining characteristics of a traumatic memory is its unwanted recurrence. Because many of Orpen’s drawings are held in sketchbooks, a researcher flipping through the pages often surprisingly comes across a patient that has appeared in earlier sketchbooks. There is no closure to these patients’ traumas because there is no “after” (healed) drawing and because patients and their injuries could reappear at any time while turning from one page to the next.

![Image 43: stevenson d 743](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/stevenson-d-743.jpg?w=348&h=426)

[Dickie Orpen,_BAPRAS D/743_(“Fitzgerald”), 1943, pen on paper, Archive of the British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive, and Aesthetic Surgeons, London]

One of Orpen’s ways of tangibly alluding to this repetitive characteristic of traumatic memory is her use of the innocuous-sounding French word “finis.” She often puts this word in the top right corner of her paper when she believed that the surgery was finished. Yet it is almost never a _true_ finish, as the same patient will pop up again in a later sketchbook. In a drawing marked February 19 th, 1943, Orpen wrote “finis.” However, another drawing of this patient was done in June of that same year. This patient, Fitzgerald[[1]](https://dfef9c9f-aa0d-434e-8b71-92ddce0f8647/#_ftn1), would undergo many more surgeries, and he appears in seven later sketchbooks, long after Orpen first wrote “finis” next to his name (and she would do so several more times). Fitzgerald endured at least twenty-three surgeries while Orpen was at the hospital—she writes “23 rd!” on her drawing of him in the fifteenth sketchbook, but he still appears in two more. He is drawn in twenty-five loose drawings and in multiple pages throughout twelve of Orpen’s twenty-six sketchbooks. Looking through these continuously is like reliving Fitzgerald’s trauma over and over again. The written compositional addition of “finis” compounded with the sketchbook format suggests to me that the trauma that Orpen depicted is a type of injury that continually haunts and returns, a wound that cannot be relegated to the past.

✚

Dissociation

Another symptom that often accompanies psychological trauma is dissociation, which occurs when normal processes, memories, or even identities are broken down and separated out from the normal progression of a personal narrative. The narrative must be reintegrated and put in the correct order for the physical and mental symptoms of psychological trauma to abate. The theory of dissociation is relevant to my archival space because Orpen’s sketchbooks are not organized in a logical progression. The boxes in the archive are often out of order, and so are the sketchbook pages. In some of these sketchbooks, Orpen seems to have used the first page that the book opened to when she walked into the operating theatre, regardless of which page had been used previously for the same patient. The images of one patient may be separated by dozens of pages or even multiple sketchbooks, as discussed with the patient Fitzgerald.

If I want to know the progression of a patient’s surgeries and recovery, it would be nearly impossible to piece together the full narrative of their stay at Orpen’s hospital without looking through every single sketchbook and loose sheet. The loose sheets might offer insight into individual surgeries, but they do not show a person’s entire history in the ward. Therefore there is no closure in almost any of these surgical cases—just as there is no closure in a dissociated traumatic memory disorder. Rather, these images are like memories of the surgical trauma that are out of order, and they cannot be moved on from because the narrative has not been fully integrated.

✚

Repression

In the section of the archive that holds Hennell’s photographs, the archivist often placed the more healed images at the top of each patient’s folder, even though this scrambled the surgery’s progression. It seems that this was done to protect the archive viewer from being caught off guard by the intensity of the photographs. But this means that “after” images appear before “before” images. Realizing the impact of the individual medical archivist in relation to these photographs made me acknowledge that the BAPRAS archive, like all others, is someone else’s interpretation of how to approach these images; not a representation of how the physical trauma or any accompanying mental distress realistically happened to the people pictured. This realization intensified my empathy with the patients in the photographs, allowing reflection on how someone else narrated, mediated, and partially repressed their traumas.

This suppression within the archive is reminiscent of British repression of mental distress during World War II. There was heavy cultural emphasis on upholding a stiff upper lip, when one would not freely express personal issues with psychological trauma or weakness. During the Blitz there were over forty thousand civilians killed and over fifty thousand injured, yet the reports on civil morale maintained that it was high, and the phrase “Britain can take it!” filled airways and conversations. The “repression” within the archive always makes me think of the repression that saturated the culture in which these patients lived. Perhaps in this milieu they would have felt their traumas too gruesome or difficult to speak about freely, or would have shied away from seeking help for them. Because these drawings and photographs show these patients in the hospital, they were obviously getting help for their physical traumas. But what of their minds?

![Image 44: Littlewood HEN:4:2:1](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/06/littlewood-hen421.jpg?w=354&h=437)

[Percy Hennell,_BAPRAS/HEN/4/2/1_, 1942, colored photograph, Archive of the British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive, and Aesthetic Surgeons, London]

✚

Secondary Traumatic Stress

Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder is a common phrase in our modern age, well known and freely (often problematically) used in everyday parlance; Secondary Traumatic Stress Disorder is a less well-known concept. It suggests that not only those who experience a traumatic event can be traumatized. Those who care for (physically and mentally) the victims of trauma, or even those who simply hear about traumatic events can be traumatized via explanation of the incident.

In my research I have encountered and learned details of myriad traumatic events: mostly bombs, shots, and burns that caused both civilians and soldiers facial injuries. The traumatic images and accompanying records that explicate these events were originally meant for a specialized, medical audience. But now people like me—whether art historians or just non-medical researchers—have these difficult surgical pictures at our fingertips in open-access archives like BAPRAS. The tightly cropped compositions and scientific context of these surgical images turn the subjects into specimens, but non-medically trained viewers will still see men and women—and this conflict between specimens and humans is part of what makes these photographs so affecting for those of us studying these images today. Orpen’s drawings, like Hennell’s photographs, are positioned between the scientific objectification of the patient and a human understanding of their trauma. But the use of color in Hennell’s photographs marks them as more modern, emotional, and “real” than Orpen’s monochrome drawings. Since color photographs are the primary medium of image-sharing today, his photographs make it seem like these are the people of my everyday, that these types of traumas could happen to the ones that I love, or that these injuries—both psychological and physical—could happen to me. Instead of distancing the trauma, as Michel Foucault argues that medical photographs do, the photographs in the BAPRAS archive, especially when combined in a collection with the more tender and interpretive Orpen drawings, bring the trauma of the Second World War into the present day.

My personal experience in the BAPRAS archive exemplifies how this transference of trauma can happen. Because I visited the archive in person and did not click through the images online, I had to “touch” the injuries of these patients, something that is only possible in a real (non-digital) archival space, and something that draws a researcher closer both physically and mentally to their objects of study. In the notes from my first visits to the archive, I remarked on the visceral, physical reaction that I had to each new patient and photograph. My emotional responses remained unexpressed to myself or to the archivists, but they transformed into legitimate physical discomfort and nausea. I found myself verbally repressing the feelings of secondary traumatization that I was having in the archive, especially since I felt that any emotional response to these images somehow would compromise my objective status as an academic. In reality, what I was feeling was that the images in the BAPRAS archive transferred the sitters’ trauma to me. This happened even though I was miles away from the hospital in which they were treated, and decades away temporally.

✚

My time in the BAPRAS archive has allowed me to ruminate on how this one space containing a traumatic history resembles the psychological trauma that we associate with the types of injuries shown in the drawings and photographs that it contains. Thinking of the BAPRAS archive, and medical archives generally, as taking on the symptoms and traits of psychological trauma has helped me to explain the emotional and mental stress that these types of collections can cause. In the BAPRAS archive I have been immersed in the chaos of traumatic injury, seeing the many surgeries over and over again as structural metaphors for the haunting loops that make up traumatic memory.

# [The Medical Narrative: Before and After](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2018/12/17/the-medical-narrative-before-and-after/)

*   Uncategorized
*   [Leave a comment](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2018/12/17/the-medical-narrative-before-and-after/#respond)

When artistic images are conceptualized as a series, the way in which the groupings are organized and the order in which the pictures are conveyed can change the communicated message of the sequence. Historical photographs and drawings of patients often use a “before and after” narrative convention—one that is more likely to be seen today in advertisements for diet pills or workout machinery. But this simple, two-part narrative is a powerful one in the medical world. It suggests to the reader that a full and total recovery has taken place between the first image and the second one. The pair of photographs or pair of drawings becomes a “spot the difference” game, with the viewer’s eyes darting back and forth between the “before” and the “after” to sort out the parts of the patient’s body or countenance that have been “fixed.” This blog post will explore the transfixing power of this convention with two examples: the facially injured of the First World War and lobotomized patients of the mid-twentieth century. Neither of the healing procedures shown in these examples are as straightforward as the constructed visual narrative may suggest. The point of this piece of writing is to highlight the way that a constructed narrative like the convention of before and after can make us think about the medical world in an over-simplified manner.

The examples used below lack the procedural middle state. The viewer is blind to the hard work of doctors and nurses, as well as the recovery work of the patients. We see no surgical incision, nor the pain and trauma that the treatment caused the patient, and we do not see the hours of recuperation. We only see the starting point, what is framed as the “bad,” and the end point, which the images unequivocally show as the healed “good.” This sets up an unquestionable dichotomy; in this simple narrative construction there is no grey area—only black and white. The narrative in these two examples of medical imagery is abridged, therefore streamlining our understanding of the patient’s experience, the doctor’s culpability, and the viewer’s responsibility.

✚

![Image 46: Deeks Comparison](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/deeks-comparison.jpg?w=730)

[Henry Tonks, _Portraits of a Wounded Soldier Before and After Treatment_, c. 1916, pastel on paper, all rights The Royal College of Surgeons of England]

Henry Tonks

I believe that these Sidcup drawings represent a really remarkable fusion of Doctor and Artist. —Dickie Orpen, _Dickie Orpen, Surgeons’ Artist_, 2008.[[1]](https://d804d5d0-5656-4951-92ce-59bdb9563b5d/#_ftn1)

In this quotation, Henry Tonks’s student Dickie Orpen (also a medical illustrator) hits on the purpose of these before and after medical images. They are products of both the artist and the doctor—a narrative approved of by the medical machine. Tonks’s work embodies this purpose more than most, as he trained as a doctor before becoming an artist and Professor at the Slade School of Art. He was best known for his World War I work that combined both of his two major skills. In these intriguing and personal artworks, Tonks created before and after portraits of facially wounded soldiers. He did this to aid the work of Sir Harold Delf Gillies, the pioneering plastic and reconstructive surgeon with whom Tonks worked.[[2]](https://d804d5d0-5656-4951-92ce-59bdb9563b5d/#_ftn2)

![Image 47: Deeks Before](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/deeks-before.jpg?w=304&h=408)

[Henry Tonks, _Portrait of a Wounded Soldier Before Treatment_, c. 1916, pastel on paper, all rights The Royal College of Surgeons of England]

The combination of the “before” and “after” portraits creates an implicit portrait of the surgeon, Sir Harold Gillies. In the implied narrative between the two pastel images, Gillies’s reparative hand looms as an important instrument of change and healing. Tonks neither portrays Gillies himself, nor the surgical process, yet the doctor’s “inventiveness, skill, and dedication” are all displayed clearly to the viewer.[[3]](https://d804d5d0-5656-4951-92ce-59bdb9563b5d/#_ftn3) One cannot help but be in awe of the transformation from a face with mangled flesh and dripping saliva to a clean, sewn up man with a barely visible scar. These portraits chiefly were meant to function as medical documentation, yet they also serve as a type of publicity for both Gillies’s aptitude at facial reconstruction and for the hope that this surgeon might bring to other victims.

![Image 48: Deeks After](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/01/deeks-after.jpg?w=255&h=342)

[Henry Tonks, _Portrait of a Wounded Soldier After Treatment_, c. 1916, pastel on paper, all rights The Royal College of Surgeons of England]

Since the focus of these images is clearly the facial reconstruction—as Tonks’s main purpose was to document the progress of the new field of plastic surgery—the myth of the surgeon who completed the reconstruction becomes an overwhelming presence. When viewed together, both figures prompt more questions about how one could repair such a prominent wound than questions about who the patient (Private Charles Deeks) is or was. When viewed together, one cannot help but focus on the changes in the face more than anything else. In this paired context Deeks’s face becomes a canvas upon which the art of the surgeon can be worked. As S. Squire Sprigge wrote in 1917, there is an art to surgery, and “nowhere is there the connection between the art of him who draws and the science of him who operates so obvious as it is in… the rehabilitation of smashed faces.”[[4]](https://d804d5d0-5656-4951-92ce-59bdb9563b5d/#_ftn4)

This portrait of the surgeon is only apparent when the two pastel images are placed side by side. The lack of temporal and physical distance makes the talent of the doctor seem grand, even magical. When a viewer can look at both images at essentially the same time, it seems impossible that such a change could happen in just a turn of the head or a flip of the page. The pairing makes Gillies’s hard work seem effortless, further elevating his status as a surgeon and the miraculous nature of his surgical advancements. Tonks’s use of pastel also aids in this interpretation, since Tonks chose this soft medium for its aptitude for portraying the contours of flesh as well as its sketch-like appearance and ability to take accurate notes of a person’s appearance.[[5]](https://d804d5d0-5656-4951-92ce-59bdb9563b5d/#_ftn5) The rapid strokes that Tonks uses in the “before” portrait, especially with Deeks’s hair, give the impression that he had to record the initial appearance of Deeks and his wound quickly, before Gillies could step in and work his surgical magic. This implication of magic-like surgery lifts Gillies and his skill onto a pedestal while also making him a main character in Tonks’s visual narrative.

✚

![Image 49: BeforeAfter2](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/BeforeAfter2.jpeg?w=730)

[Case 123 in: Walter Freeman and James W. Watts, _Psychosurgery: In the Treatment of Mental Disorders and Intractable Pain_, 2 nd ed. (Oxford, UK: Blackwell Scientific Publications, 1950)]

Lobotomy Patients

Prefrontal lobotomy is beginning to give us some insight into the intellectual-emotional mechanisms that are such a potent factor in human behavior. —Walter Freeman and James W. Watts, _Pscyhosurgery: In the Treatment of mental Disorders and Intractable Pain_, 1950.[[6]](https://d804d5d0-5656-4951-92ce-59bdb9563b5d/#_ftn6)

Physicians Walter Freeman and Watts use the imagery in their book _Psychosurgery_ to corroborate the insights that they alluded to above, a quotation that concludes their introduction. Freeman is known for proselytizing about the benefits of lobotomies and riding around the United States in his “Lobotomobile,” performing the now-disgraced surgery on vulnerable people who were deemed mentally ill, lethargic, or socially unacceptable. A lobotomy is a neurosurgical operation that severs connections in the brain, leaving bastardized remnants of the patient’s (or, victim’s) personality, responsiveness, and intelligence. It often resulted in immediate death, later suicide, and, of course, severe brain damage.

Two examples of “healed” patients show the extent to which photographs in this book extended the reparative narrative for which Freeman and Watts hoped. The first is of a man operated on in 1942, described as “perplexed, unable to solve the simplest problem.” Once the lobotomy has occurred, he’s labelled thus: “Ten days after operation. He was no longer troubled by his obsessions, and seemed rather pleased with himself.”[[7]](https://d804d5d0-5656-4951-92ce-59bdb9563b5d/#_ftn7) Not only are the before and the after photographs framed in such a way to make the “healed” patient seem more confident and masculine, but there are props within these photographs that elevate that narrative. In the before photograph, this “perplexed” individual is shown with glasses, indicating a physical fault (bad eyesight) beyond the one that the surgeons are meant to fix. In the second photograph, the patient is shown without glasses, implying that his eyesight was fixed as well as his personality. The cigar is another important prop. It dangles jauntily (and, from today’s perspective, quite comically) from the patient’s lips. It connotes masculinity, vitality, and a cool factor absent in the earlier photograph. These images therefore suggest that a person lacking these three elements of a personality can acquire them through the outlined lobotomy procedure. And as with Tonks’s drawings, the simple two-step narrative suggests that this was a simple, easy procedure—something that modern viewers know is not the truth.

![Image 50: BeforeAfter4](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/12/BeforeAfter4.jpeg?w=730)

[Case 162 in: Walter Freeman and James W. Watts, _Psychosurgery: In the Treatment of Mental Disorders and Intractable Pain_, 2 nd ed. (Oxford, UK: Blackwell Scientific Publications, 1950)]

A second example in _Psychosurgery_ is Case 162, from 1943. He is shown changing miraculously from looking “…like he smelled something bad” to having a more relaxed countenance.[[8]](https://d804d5d0-5656-4951-92ce-59bdb9563b5d/#_ftn8) What this contrast shows, in addition to the previous example, is how the authors and photographers of this book attempted to capture a change not only visually but also temperamentally. The artistic process of either Tonks’s drawings or these photographs is supposed to go beyond skin deep to elucidate the power of the doctor and their cutting-edge procedures.

✚

Conclusion

Both plastic facial reconstructions and lobotomies were new fields of surgery at the time that these drawings and photographs were made. Therefore, the visual language that defines these procedures is doubly important, as these images (circulated at least within the surgical communities if not larger audiences) were tasked with immediately conveying the successful and appealing nature of the operations. These images also convey the power of the surgeons who worked on these patients: Gillies, Freeman, and Watts. To accomplish these visual aims, the two examples of medicalized pairings discussed in this blog post provide a straightforward narrative of healing and reconstruction. We know that this is not the full truth of the procedures and hardships that these patients underwent: facial reconstruction patients were often left with scars across their faces even if they had been deemed “healed” by their surgeons; lobotomy patients were left as human vegetables, their agency taken away with them as well as bits of their brains. As these two examples show, the order and number in which medical drawings and photographs are presented can matter just as much as the visual content within the images themselves.

✚

# [Exhibition Review: Aubrey Beardsley at Tate Britain](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2020/08/26/exhibition-review-aubrey-beardsley-at-tate-britain/)

*   Uncategorized
*   [Leave a comment](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2020/08/26/exhibition-review-aubrey-beardsley-at-tate-britain/#respond)

This exhibition review was first posted on the blog page for the Aubrey Beardsley Society. You can find that original post [here](https://ab2020.org/exhibition-review-aubrey-beardsley-at-tate-britain/).

✚

I must start this review with a disclaimer regarding my academic background, which may explain the approach that I take to Aubrey Beardsley’s oeuvre and the recently re-opened Tate Britain exhibition. I am an art historian, but I specialize in medical and surgical art, with a particular personal interest in anything considered ‘morbid’. Therefore, when entering the Tate, I found myself drawn to the elements of this show that dealt with illness and all themes and images that were grotesque, taboo, and decaying. Perhaps this focus also had something to do with the fact that this was my first visit to a museum since lockdown had lifted and, as with many of us, illness has been at the forefront of my mind for several months.

![Image 2: Beardsley Photo](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/beardsley-photo.jpg?w=306&h=437)

Frederick Henry Evans,_Aubrey Beardsley_, platinum print, 1894, NPG P115 © National Portrait Gallery, London

As someone working within the medical humanities, before visiting this show I was most familiar with stories and images of Beardsley’s gaunt, lithe, tuberculosis-stricken body, and with the mythologising of his illness and untimely death at age twenty-five. His death is often romanticised, as his story suits the dramatic tragedy of a typical male ‘great artist’ narrative. But, as befits the reputation and image of someone as revered today within the queer community as Aubrey Beardsley, depictions and descriptions of his disease, tuberculosis, were entwined with feminine beauty, frustrated passion, and drooping passivity in the late Victorian period; this is a conceptualisation of the disease that I first came across in Susan Sontag’s _Illness as Metaphor_.[[1]](https://ab2020.org/exhibition-review-aubrey-beardsley-at-tate-britain/#_ftn1) Beardsley was diagnosed with tuberculosis at age seven, but, as was often the case, the symptoms only erupted years later to become the haemorrhages that eventually killed him.

![Image 3: Beardsley Child at Mother's Bed](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/beardsley-child-at-mothers-bed.jpg?w=233&h=441)

Aubrey Beardsley,_Child at Mother’s Bed_, 1892, pen and Indian ink on white wove paper, Mrs Margaret Reade, Torquay, UK

Like this languishing, latent, lustful Victorian perception of tuberculosis, this exhibition is a slow, but beautiful, burn – one that is expressed in fits and starts. Beautiful, because of the undeniable quality of Beardsley’s line and compositional eye; slow, because there were points at which it felt like this show paused and diverted away from the truly explosive narrative of Beardsley’s unusual and often grotesque artistic power. Sontag describes tuberculosis as ‘a disease of extreme contrasts,’ in which the patient ‘is wracked by coughs, then sinks back, recovers breath, breathes normally; then coughs again.’[[2]](https://ab2020.org/exhibition-review-aubrey-beardsley-at-tate-britain/#_ftn2) My response to Beardsley’s drawings in this show felt delayed at several instances, like tubercular symptoms. The most glaring point at which the excitement goes latent is in a central room of the show that displayed photographs and artistic representations of and by Beardsley’s circle. The walls of this space were painted orange – a colour that the curators may have hoped (in vain) could subconsciously drum up a thrill similar to that of the lurid and erotic yellow of the literary periodical that Beardsley illustrated, _The Yellow Book_. This room concentrated on Beardsley’s friends and family, taking the viewer out of the fantastical narrative of grotesque decadence that was being built up in previous rooms. These paintings and drawings paled in comparison to Beardsley’s own production.

In contrast, the symptoms of decadence and perversion erupt most violently and satisfyingly in an eggplant-coloured alcove (perhaps a nod to that most suggestive of emojis?!) within the show’s large final room. These three purple walls are introduced with a content warning: this space holds Beardsley’s _Lysistrata_ drawings, the most overtly sexual of his oeuvre, although sexualised details and explicit phalluses appear several times in earlier rooms in this show. The placement of this alcove fits with my loose concept of this show as tubercular, as it is just before the end that the ugly (but beautiful, as tuberculosis is historically depicted) head of disease finally rears the full extent of its nastiness. In this context, however, the nastiness is what we, as viewers, have longed for all along.

![Image 4: Beardsley Lysistrata](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/beardsley-lysistrata.jpg?w=350&h=467)

Aubrey Beardsley,_Lysistrata Defending the Acropolis_, from _The Lysistrata of Aristophanes_ (1896), ca. 1929 (printed and published). Victoria and Albert Museum, London

Returning to the colours that dominated this show, and their connections to illness, there was a subtle yellow theme throughout the exhibition. The yellow walls in the show’s second room ostensibly hint at the forthcoming exploration of _The Yellow Book_, perhaps Beardsley’s most famous contribution to British visual culture. But in addition to this, the association of points to a further connotation of the colour yellow: it can be likened to the particular hue of coughed-up sputum that suggests a lung infection diagnosis. The colour of the walls also reminds viewers of another late Victorian artistic rumination on illness and confinement: Charlotte Perkin Gilman’s _The Yellow Wallpaper._

![Image 5: Beardsley Yellow Book](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/beardsley-yellow-book.jpg?w=327&h=394)

Aubrey Beardsley, cover design for _The Yellow Book_, vol. I, 1894. The British Library, London

The last room of this exhibition suggests that the ‘sickness’ that Beardsley began during his lifetime has continued to spread and to infect millions of people around the world. One of my favourite works from this final space, _In Memoriam_(c. 1923) by an unknown artist, imagines a death-bed scene, compiled of Beardsley’s own characters – both the fashionable and the grotesque. The time-tested fixation on the taboo elements of his work, as well as his distinctive forms and lines, shows that the Beardsley disease is here to stay, with no vaccine _en route_, or, for that matter, desired.

# [Dangle ‘Ums and Marsupial Pouches: World War II Plastic Surgery Techniques and Humour](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2020/07/15/dangle-ums-and-marsupial-pouches-world-war-ii-plastic-surgery-techniques-and-humour/)

*   Uncategorized
*   [Leave a comment](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2020/07/15/dangle-ums-and-marsupial-pouches-world-war-ii-plastic-surgery-techniques-and-humour/#respond)

This post originally appeared on the Surgery & Emotion blog([link](http://www.surgeryandemotion.com/blog)). Check out the Surgery & Emotion project’s amazing publications ([link here)](http://www.surgeryandemotion.com/publications) or follow them on Twitter ([link](https://twitter.com/SurgicalEmotion)).

✚

It’s almost a cliché to acknowledge that humour is used in difficult situations to defuse tensions or to alter the mood.But in these last few months, we’ve seen a proliferation of jokes regarding the Covid-19 crisis: most frequently, through memes and tweets, such as the many humorous takes on the government’s official coronavirus advice and graphics. ([link](https://twitter.com/Cain_Unable/status/1259357834069901312))

I’ve found this interesting in the context of my research on the visual culture and humour of plastic surgery during the Second World War. Humour, in both images and words, thrived in the plastics wards. But here I’d like to focus on two particular surgical technologies that were used to treat patients with facial injuries and burns: the skin flap and the tube pedicle.

A skin flap is exactly what it sounds like: a surgically detached flap of skin that can be transferred to another area. For a tube pedicle, the skin is rolled to prevent infection, and both ends of the tube are attached to the body to ensure blood flow before one end is removed and connected to the injury so that it can be sculpted into a new nose or chin. Thousands of drawings and photographs were made during the Second World War of these surgical techniques. But there were also images of and comments on these tubes and flaps that play on their strangeness through humour.

Tube pedicles became a ubiquitous tool for facial reconstruction during the First World War. Harold Gillies remarked on them often in his 1957 book _The Principles and Art of Plastic Surgery_. As the most prominent plastic surgeon in Britain in the twentieth century, Gillies’s sense of humour contributed significantly to the culture of the field. In his typically humorous and exaggerated manner, Gillies wrote that his World War I plastic surgery ward in Sidcup ‘soon resembled the jungles of Burma, teeming with dangling pedicles.’[[1]](http://www.surgeryandemotion.com/blog/view/dangle-ums-and-marsupial-pouches-world-war-ii-plastic-surgery-techniques-and-humour#_ftn1) This incongruous description jars with our understanding of the tube pedicle as an invasive, uncomfortable object for the patient to whom it is attached. Gillies commented on the tube pedicle again about a hundred pages later in the book:

If all the tube pedicles that I have made and those my assistants have made were laid end to end, by calculations at two and a half pedicles per week, they would string like sausages from Buckingham Palace down the Mall, straight on through the Admiralty Arch to Trafalgar Square and half-way up Nelson’s monument. It is my ambition that before my last pedicle is made we will reach the top of this famous pinnacle with at least one pedicle left to go into the Admiral’s palate.[[2]](http://www.surgeryandemotion.com/blog/view/dangle-ums-and-marsupial-pouches-world-war-ii-plastic-surgery-techniques-and-humour#_ftn2)

Gillies’s ability to make jokes like this suggests either that he could detach himself—physically, emotionally, or temporally—from the suffering inflicted by this surgical technique, or that the humour is itself a manifestation of Gillies’s own trauma. There is also the possibility that Gillies, and other surgeons, could have utilised humour as a coercive, perhaps patronising, tactic: one that could make their patients feel like their traumas were minimal or less serious. Whatever the justification for this tone, Gillies successfully infuses the tube pedicle with humour through his animated language.

Perhaps surprisingly, facial surgery patients themselves made similar comments about their tube pedicles. Some patients gave this unsightly and uncomfortable fleshly apparatus a humorous nickname: ‘dangle ‘um.’ There was a social group in Scotland, similar to one in England (the Guinea Pig Club), that was formed around this particular trial of facial reconstruction, called The Dangle ‘Ums Club.[[3]](http://www.surgeryandemotion.com/blog/view/dangle-ums-and-marsupial-pouches-world-war-ii-plastic-surgery-techniques-and-humour#_ftn3) This language trivialises and infantilises the tube pedicle—such a light-hearted name lessens the fear of and aversion to the surgically constructed roll of flesh.

![Image 7: fs](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/fs.jpg?w=323&h=426)

Dickie Orpen, BAPRAS/DSB 7.26, pencil on paper, Archives of the British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive and Aesthetic Surgeons, London.

A similar goal is met in a drawing by the artist Dickie Orpen, who was based in St Albans at Hill End Hospital’s plastic surgery ward during the Second World War. In this image, a combination skin flap and tube pedicle is being transposed. Even though this is a highly specialised image, meant to show the numbered steps of this surgical procedure, it is also transgressive in its sense of humour. In the centre of the image, the surgical artist has ‘christened’ the roll of flesh with the name ‘Angus,’ dating it January 13th, 1943, 2:55 pm. There is room in this page, and in the surgical ward as a whole, for play and humour in the face of pain and distress.

Like Orpen, Gillies used images to imbue tube pedicles and skin flaps with humour. Gillies’s 1957 book is incredibly odd; not only is it written in a humorous tone (evident in the tube pedicle quotations above), but the descriptions of some truly horrific facial injuries and full-body burns are often accompanied by irreverent cartoons and photographs. One reviewer called it ‘a combination of autobiography, an unorthodox text, an informal reference book, filled with the most astounding array of illustrations … as well as a complete drama in the development of plastic surgery.’[[4]](http://www.surgeryandemotion.com/blog/view/dangle-ums-and-marsupial-pouches-world-war-ii-plastic-surgery-techniques-and-humour#_ftn1)

![Image 8: Gillies, Harold, and D. Ralph Millard, Jr. The Principles and Art of Plastic Surgery, vol. 1, preface, np, 1957, published by Butterworth & Co. ](https://i0.wp.com/www.surgeryandemotion.com/content/images/Gillies_1957_Prologue.JPG)
Gillies, Harold, and D. Ralph Millard, Jr._The Principles and Art of Plastic Surgery_, vol. 1, preface, np, 1957, published by Butterworth & Co.

In the prologue, there is an image of a man with a long nose with birds perched upon it, drawn by the artist and nonsense poet Edward Lear (who happened to be Gillies’s great-uncle). The poem below it humorously states that this nose could be stolen and used as a tube pedicle. But perhaps the strangest image in this book is in the section on ‘Direct Flaps,’ on a page describing ‘The “Marsupial” Flap.’ Here, Gillies inserted a photograph of a surgeon into the ‘pouch’ that the flap makes around a real patient’s abdomen. In my research on this topic and this period, it seems that there are few lines that humour cannot cross in plastic surgery, as even an ostensibly serious publication by two established surgeons can have a visual joke like this within it.

![Image 9: Gillies, Harold, and D. Ralph Millard, Jr. The Principles and Art of Plastic Surgery, vol. 1, p. 151, 1957, published by Butterworth & Co. [full page and detail as featured image] ](https://i0.wp.com/www.surgeryandemotion.com/content/images/Gillies_1957_Marsupial_Flap_2.JPG)
Gillies, Harold, and D. Ralph Millard, Jr._The Principles and Art of Plastic Surgery_, vol. 1, p. 151, 1957, published by Butterworth & Co. [detail of this image is at the top of the page, as the Featured Image]

As I’ve alluded to above, the question of _who_ is making these visual and verbal jokes matters. There are ethical and personal differences between patients making fun of their own faces, surgical artists adding humour to the depicted procedures, and surgeons making light of their practice. Further thought and research will have to be given to these questions of coercion, agency, and humour in a longer piece of writing, but this blog post hopefully begins the conversation.

In their book _Operative Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery_ (1980), John N. Barron and Magdy N. Saad provide a potted etymology of the word ‘surgery’:

‘The word _surgery_ in English is derived from the older word form _chirurgery_, related to the French _chirugie_ and Latin _chirurgia_… Similarly, the word _surgeon_ is related to the Greek _kheirougos_. The Greek word contains two roots; _khier_, a hand and _ergon_, which means work or activity… In effect therefore, surgery means handworking and a surgeon is a handworker. Although the word _kheirourgos_ could indicate any handworker, its use has been largely restricted to the medical sense for some 2000 years, as have all European words and derivatives.’ [[1]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn1)

The focus in Barron and Saad’s definition here is the hands-on reality of surgery. Their emphasis is on the craftmanship of the work, and, in this instance, surgery is not the cerebral, detached, scientific profession that it is sometimes cast as being. Much of the visual language surrounding surgery—particularly plastic surgery—compares the work of the surgeon to the work of the artist. This idea of being a ‘handworker’ provides a concrete, visual tie between these two occupations, and this blog post will spotlight a few fascinating examples of hands being conceived of as the focus of genius and as the key marker of the practitioner’s identity—in both of these seemingly disparate jobs.

Many surgeons are and were amateur artists in their spare time, making cartoons, sculptures, or paintings; several of the practical and linguistic elements of the field point to this fact. [[2]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn2) For example, today’s plastic surgery tools—such as those with the ‘Barron’ handle, named for the surgeon quoted above—have octagonal rather than round handles, which allow for quick, precise, and artistic rotations. [[3]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn3) Textbooks and articles on plastic surgery include ‘art’ or ‘sculpture’ in their titles as well as hand-drawn illustrations from surgical artists. [[4]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn4) Saad describes his patients as his pieces of art, worthy of being hung like a painting or placed like a sculpture in the cluttered halls of the Chelsea Arts Club. [[5]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn5) Additionally, a prominent surgeon who worked with John Barron was considered to be ‘an artist and a craftsman’ when it came to sculpting live tissue in a surgical reconstruction. [[6]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn6)

[![Image 11: Barbara Hepworth The Artist's Hand](https://i0.wp.com/morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/barbara-hepworth-the-artists-hand.png?w=395&h=246&ssl=1)](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2020/04/14/handworkers-art-surgery-and-the-hands-that-craft/barbara-hepworth-the-artists-hand/)

[![Image 12: Barbara Hepworth Hand II horizontal](https://i0.wp.com/morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/barbara-hepworth-hand-ii-horizontal.png?w=327&h=246&ssl=1)](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2020/04/14/handworkers-art-surgery-and-the-hands-that-craft/barbara-hepworth-hand-ii-horizontal/)

[Figure 1:Barbara Hepworth,_The Artist’s Hand_, 1943-4, Tate.]

[Figure 2:Barbara Hepworth,_Hand II (horizontal)_, 1950, private collection.]

The focus on the artistry and genius of the surgeon’s hand does not stop at plastic surgery. As many mid-century surgeons saw their surgery as sculpting human flesh, it is particularly fascinating to see the relationship between a renowned sculptor (Barbara Hepworth) and a well-known surgeon (Norman Capener). In 1947, Capener, an orthopedic surgeon, invited Hepworth to sketch his operations, having met her when Hepworth’s daughter had been ill. I previously wrote about Hepworth’s surgical drawings that result from these hours of observation in the blog post ‘Barbara Hepworth’s Hospital Drawings: Sculptural, Surgical, Tactile, Haptic’ from March 2018. Some of the discussion of the importance of hands in Hepworth’s surgical works can also be found there. As a sculptor who used the practice of ‘direct carving’ to create her works, Hepworth was particularly focused on the power of the artist’s hand and the scope of work that could be created with one’s hands. In a speech given to surgeons in 1953, Hepworth stated, ‘As I became more accustomed to the various operations I began to realize how profoundly important from an artist’s point of view the expression of the human hand is. Not only is it the most revealing and expressive part of the human body—it is also the visible extension of the brain and feeling generally.’ [[7]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn7) Through her work in operating theatres, Hepworth discovered the parallels of her own use of hands and touch to that of surgeons. Around 1943, Hepworth made a cast of her left hand, which she called her ‘thinking’ hand, titled _The Artist’s Hand_(Fig. 1). [[8]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn8) And after spending two years observing Capener’s surgeries, Hepworth cast a bronze sculpture of his hand entitled _Hand II (horizontal)_ (Fig. 2). By creating these similar casts, Hepworth elevated the status of the tactile skills of both surgeon and sculptor, turning the physical conduit of that skill into a work of art itself. This must have been a particularly affecting exchange for Capener, who was an amateur sculptor himself, to have his hand depicted by such a prominent sculptor. Capener’s wife donated his _Clasped Hands_(Fig. 3) sculpture to the Royal College of Surgeons in 1976. According to an article covering this donation, Capener ‘was always keenly interested in hands, in surgery, pottery, and all forms of craftsmanship’—as was his friend and collaborator, Barbara Hepworth. [[9]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn9)

![Image 13: Norman Capener Clasped Hands](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/norman-capener-clasped-hands.jpg?w=404&h=408)

[Figure 3:Norman Capener,_Clasped Hands_, c. 1951, Royal College of Surgeons.]

Images of surgeons’ hands can be used for more obviously self-serving purposes, as seen in the colour photographs that Percy Hennell took of two prominent British plastic surgeons Harold Gillies (Fig. 4) and Archibald McIndoe (Fig. 5). The striking image of Gillies’s gloved hands against a deep green background served as the cover for his 1957 book _The Principles and Art of Plastic Surgery_. Like a sculptor or a painter, Gillies gingerly and expertly holds the tools of his trade. The aesthetic, slightly asymmetrical composition that Hennell has created adds to the artistic connotations of the plastic surgeon’s professsion. The photograph of McIndoe’s hands is quite different from the one of Gillies, as it is not as static nor as precisely composed. Rather, this image of McIndoe’s hands touts the stability and confidence of the surgeon’s hands. With something as sensitive as a patient’s eye, and with a small dropper tool, McIndoe’s gloved hands are precise and sure in their movements. It is also telling that even though her eye is being opened by force by McIndoe’s gloved hand, the patient (perhaps sedated) appears calm and unworried by the surgeon’s intrusion.

[![Image 14: HEN:11:5](https://i0.wp.com/morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/hen115.jpg?w=352&h=448&ssl=1)](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2020/04/14/handworkers-art-surgery-and-the-hands-that-craft/hen115/)

[![Image 15: McIndoe's Hands Downloaded](https://i0.wp.com/morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/mcindoes-hands-downloaded.jpg?w=370&h=448&ssl=1)](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/2020/04/14/handworkers-art-surgery-and-the-hands-that-craft/mcindoes-hands-downloaded/)

[Figure 4: Percy Hennell,_Harold Gillies’s Hands_, c. 1957, Archives of the British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive, and Aesthetic Surgeons, London]

[Figure 5: Percy Hennell,_Archibald McIndoe’s Hands_, Archives of the British Association of Plastic, Reconstructive, and Aesthetic Surgeons, London]

These examples of Capener’s, Gillies’s, and McIndoe’s hands show that surgeon’s hands were of interest in artistic representations. But even when the hand is not the overt focus in a piece of surgical art, it can end up being what the artist emphasizes or what viewers pick up on when observing the piece. One example is William Orpen’s portrait of the surgeon Ivor Back (Fig. 6) from 1926. The tight, dark gloves are similar to those worn by Gillies and McIndoe in their hand portraits. And yet this portrait is about the entirety of the surgeon, and is not specifically focused on his hands. But by painting most of the composition in light colors to correspond with the doctor’s surgical dress, Orpen has drawn the viewer’s eyes immediately to Back’s hands and head. In _Sir William Orpen: Artist and Man_(1932), P. G. Konody and Sidney Dark write that in this painting, the ‘form and weight of the body are felt through the white overall, although the material is far from pliant or clinging. A superb passage of expressive painting is found in the hand. Although it is covered by a brown rubber glove and shown in a limp state of complete relaxation, it is unmistakably a capable hand, firm and sensitive and dependable in the professional use of the scalpel.’ [[10]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn10) Much of these descriptors could also be applied to either of the gloved hands in Hennell’s photographs.

![Image 16: Orpen The Surgeon Ivor Back](https://morbidarthistory.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/orpen-the-surgeon-ivor-back.jpg?w=730)

[Figure 6:William Orpen,_The Surgeon (Ivor Back)_, 1926, The Hunterian Museum at the Royal College of Surgeons]

Moving on from surgeons, there are many examples of artists’ hands being the focuses of visual works or being thought of as the nexus from which genius springs. But there is an interesting example of William Orpen’s hand—the hand that emphasized the quiet strength and skillful pliability of a surgeon’s hand—being lauded and studied as the most important part of the artist’s body. Noel Jacquin, a leading figure in British palmistry during the twentieth century, christened Orpen’s hand as ‘a perfect example of the artistic hand.’ [[11]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn11) Jacquin had several reasons for why Orpen’s hand contained artistic genius, quoting attributes like ‘conical finger tips’ as the elements that held the key to Orpen’s skill. While palmistry is a disproved pseudoscience, the twentieth-century fascination with the hand of the artist, and the hand of the surgeon, remains. It is understandable for people to see a kernel of intrinsic talent living within these fingertips, bones, and muscles. Of course, at the very base of it, art historian Mary Hunter sums up the practical side of it best: ‘Both surgical and artistic practice requires a connection of mental and manual ability and expert hand-eye coordination; drawing, painting, sculpting, and performing surgery are all visual and haptic activities that utilize similar specialized knowledge.’ [[12]](https://4f155eb9-8516-4548-ac60-72adf5bb04ef/#_ftn12) Hunter’s chapter ‘Art and Surgery: The Expert Hands of Artists and Surgeons’ in the _Palgrave Handbook of the History of Surgery_(2018) is an excellent source to read for a more in-depth look at the theoretical implications of the parallels between artists’ and surgeons’ hands.
