## Oct. 5**Who’s the Shockingest of Them All?**

#### By JENNIFER SCHUESSLER

More than two weeks ago, at the beginning of this project, we asked readers to vote in an entirely unscientific poll of the most shocking artistic event of the past century. Now the votes are in.

Sorry, Elvis’s swiveling hips, Lenny Bruce’s dirty mouth and Karen Finley’s chocolate-smeared body. The biggest outrage of the last hundred years, according to a full third of voters, was the 1999 [“Sensation” show at the Brooklyn Museum](https://www.nytimes.com/1999/10/05/arts/critic-s-notebook-a-madonna-s-many-meanings-in-the-art-world.html "Notebook about the show"). That show, featuring the work of shock-seeking [Young British Artists](http://www.artfact.com/fine-art-genre/young-british-artists-yba-xgfwjr62fb "Examples of their work") like Damien Hirst and Tracey Emin, got a harsh review from Mayor Rudolph W. Giuliani, who, singling out Chris Ofili’s painting of a black Madonna that included elephant dung, dismissed it as “sick stuff” and tried to cut off city funds for the museum.

![Image 2](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2012/10/04/arts/04shock-sensation/04shock-sensation-blog480.jpg)

Associated Press

“Sensation” was displayed at the Brooklyn Museum from Oct. 2, 1999 to Jan. 9, 2000.

Many of the readers and writers for The New York Times who participated in this project agreed that shock is all about context. And this discussion began in the midst of a wholly unanticipated context: [the outcry over “Innocence of Muslims,”](http://topics.nytimes.com/top/reference/timestopics/subjects/i/innocence_of_muslims_riots/index.html?8qa "Articles about controversy") the anti-Islam video that sparked violent riots across the Muslim world. Closer to home the news that Andres Serrano’s infamous 1987 photograph “Piss Christ” [would be exhibited again in New York](http://www.guardian.co.uk/artanddesign/2012/sep/28/andres-serrano-piss-christ-new-york "Article about exhibition") had some Christians calling on President Obama to denounce the photo as strongly as he denounced the video. (On the show’s opening day William Donohue, the president of the Catholic League and a veteran of the fight over “Sensation,” [released his own video](https://www.nytimes.com/2012/09/29/nyregion/catholic-leader-turned-away-at-exhibit-he-deemed-offensive.html "Article about William Donahue") showing a bobblehead Obama doll submerged in feces-colored water, declaring, “The cultural and political elite are basically secularist; they don’t believe in God. This is their god.”)

Many participants in this forum cast a weary eye on what sometimes passes for shock these days. Roberta Smith, The Times’s co-chief art critic, wrote that people sometimes “deliberately choose to be shocked and to use their shock in divisive, irresponsible, sensationalizing, not to mention politically manipulative ways.”

Jon Caramanica, in [a round table of pop music critics](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/arts/art-shock.html?ref=arts "Pop music critics’ forum"), put it more bluntly: “There’s something hopelessly middle class about shock.”

But still shock persists, sometimes in surprising places. Stravinsky’s “Rite of Spring,” whose [riotous opening night in 1913](https://www.nytimes.com/2012/09/16/arts/shock-me-if-you-can.html?pagewanted=all "Article about premiere") inspired this project, came in third in our poll, behind “A Clockwork Orange” but well ahead of the “Saw” torture-porn franchise. It’s an impressive showing for a work that, as my colleague Daniel J. Wakin [pointed out](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/arts/art-shock.html?ref=arts "Article about New York Philharmonic performance"), notably failed to cause any fuss when it was performed by the New York Philharmonic last month. Will today’s outrages outlive their hackle-raising 15 minutes of fame? Call me in another 100 years, and let’s talk.

## Oct. 4**Critics’ Forum: The Shocking Power of Great Art**

_Four critics for The New York Times — Roberta Smith, Ben Brantley, A.O. Scott and Alastair Macaulay — are chatting about the role of shock in art: how it works, how it has changed and why it’s still necessary. Jennifer Schuessler moderates._

**JENNIFER SCHUESSLER, REPORTER:** In our last round we talked about the ways in which shock is a matter of social choice. As Alastair put it, “Outrage isn’t just instinctive; it too is an act, a form of performance.” And sometimes we change the script: what was once shocking, whether it’s [“The Rite of Spring”](https://www.nytimes.com/2012/09/16/arts/shock-me-if-you-can.html?pagewanted=all "Article about \"Rite of Spring\" ") or [“Life of Brian,”](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vVHhg67RVd4 "Trailer for \"Life of Brian\" ") becomes deeply pleasurable. But sometimes what’s shocking just remains shocking — at least to some people. What are we to make of the desire to keep fighting the same old fights over art?

**ROBERTA SMITH, CO-CHIEF ART CRITIC:** I agree with Ben and Alastair that shock is wildly contextual. Also that people deliberately choose to be shocked and to use their shock in divisive, irresponsible, sensationalizing, not to mention politically manipulative ways, as in the culture wars that erupted around the [National Endowment of the Arts’ support of the work of Robert Mapplethorpe](https://www.nytimes.com/1989/06/14/arts/corcoran-to-foil-dispute-drops-mapplethorpe-show.html?pagewanted=all&src=pm "Article about the controversy"), Andres Serrano, David Wojnarowicz and others.

Duchamp’s [“Nude Descending a Staircase, No. 2”](http://www.philamuseum.org/collections/permanent/51449.html "An image") was exhibited without fuss in Barcelona and Paris before causing a furor in [the 1913 Armory Show](http://www.askart.com/askart/interest/new_york_armory_show_of_1913s_1.aspx?id=15 "A description of the show") in the United States — a high-profile exhibition in a country with little exposure to Cubism. (In addition more than one critic has noted that reaction to the painting would have been much more muted if it had a more neutral title, like “Study in Green and Brown.”) The painting that caused the outcry when Charles Saatchi’s “Sensation” exhibition was seen in London was not [Chris Ofili’s “Holy Virgin Mary,”](https://www.nytimes.com/1999/10/05/arts/critic-s-notebook-a-madonna-s-many-meanings-in-the-art-world.html "Article about New York show") which as [I noted earlier](https://www.nytimes.com/1989/06/14/arts/corcoran-to-foil-dispute-drops-mapplethorpe-show.html?pagewanted=all&src=pm "Critics’ earlier discussion") was vilified by some during the show’s New York stop, but [Marcus Harvey’s large portrait of the British child murderer Myra Hindley](http://hscvisualartresources.wordpress.com/2012/07/10/marcus-harvey/ "Images of Marcus Harvey’s work"), who was unknown to most New Yorkers. Forget the fact that the Harvey work was a derivative fusion of Andy Warhol and Chuck Close. It and even the Duchamp function as vessels or triggers; they are not lastingly or implicitly shocking. (Sorry, Duchamp.)

Yet even discounting the ways that we adjust and become more open to great works that initially shock us, I still think some retain some of their power to shock because it is more inherent in their form, whether it is Lear’s blinding of Gloucester or the splintered shapes of [Picasso’s “Demoiselles d’Avignon”](http://www.moma.org/collection/object.php?object_id=79766 "\"Demoiselles d’Avignon\" ") or — to choose a less pictorially violent work that is also at the Museum of Modern Art — the glorious red expanse of [Barnett Newman’s “Vir Heroicus Sublimis.”](http://www.moma.org/collection/object.php?object_id=79250 "Virs Heroicus Sublimis")

But here I may be again blurring the definition of shock that [Ben earlier made so convincingly specific](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/arts/art-shock.html?ref=arts#/#critics3 "Earlier critics’ forum"). But that is what I’m left with, the feeling that a form of shock is to some degree, however small, present in most aesthetic experiences. It’s not the kind of public, performed shock that greeted the first performance of “The Rite of Spring” by any means. But, unfortunately, staged “shock” can rear its head at any time, when the occasion permits and someone has a need. People are only human.

I experienced two very different performance pieces at [documenta 13](http://d13.documenta.de/#welcome/ "Web site for documenta 13") this summer. One, mentioned in [Jenny’s introduction to this discussion](https://www.nytimes.com/2012/09/16/arts/shock-me-if-you-can.html?pagewanted=all "Introduction to Shock Value") in Arts & Leisure, was [a work by the French choreographer Jérôme Bel](http://tagr.tv/2012/documenta13-jerome-bel/) that involved several adults with learning disabilities who, after introducing themselves, each danced or danced and sang to the pop music of their choice with an intense and contagious passion. I started shocked and disoriented and ended up completely caught up in it and grateful for what it revealed to me about what is often called “our common humanity.” It taught me about life in a very direct, but also a rather documentary form.

The other piece was by Tino Sehgal and involved visitors simply walking into and finding their way around a darkened room in which about 20 performers were singing, moving and occasionally talking. It was total immersion in a sense, and the space felt literally, palpably electrifying. It was as if they were enacting the life force not of life but of art itself. The shock I felt here was much more manageable and familiar, but in some ways it gave me more to think about in terms of art. Both works and the shocks they caused remain exceptionally vivid to me, not the least, I suspect, for the ways they play off each other.

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=glIK9N0EQ1k)

**BEN BRANTLEY, CHIEF THEATER CRITIC:** Roberta has perfectly crystallized the essential distinction that we’ve been flirting with from the beginning of this discussion. The shock in art that makes headlines is often the most superficial kind of shock — something that people _choose_ to be offended by because it violates their principles of faith or politics or whatever ideological system they use to give order to the world.

In these instances people often aren’t responding to the work of art itself but the idea of it. This is borne out by the (to me) embarrassing fact that in many of these cases the righteously shocked have not even seen the work in question. Movies, plays, art exhibitions (see Roberta on the “Sensation” show) and performance-art works have all been subjected to editorial attacks and picket lines by protesters who have had no firsthand experience of them.

Take the sad case of Terrence McNally’s “Corpus Christi,” which portrayed Jesus as a gay man. That notion so outraged so many that the Manhattan Theater Club had to install [metal detectors](https://www.nytimes.com/1998/10/14/arts/theater-review-nice-young-man-and-disciples-appeal-for-tolerance.html?pagewanted=all&src=pm "Review of the play") for the play’s premiere in 1998. And, honestly, it was such a boring, gentle play that it would have sunk without a trace had it not received so much publicity from its detractors.

![Image 3](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2012/10/05/arts/05shock-corpus/05shock-corpus-articleLarge.jpg)

Michelle V. Agins/The New York Times

Protests against the 1998 run of “Corpus Christi.”

Then there’s the shock that, as Roberta and Alastair have said, is inherent in great art. I’m still romantic enough to think that the function of art is to let us see, if only for a second, the world without veils, one that exists in a pure state of concentrated beauty and ugliness. If I may use some biblical quotations without giving offense, I’d argue that most of our lives we spend seeing “through a glass darkly,” while art brings us “face to face” with (switching references here) “the real thing.” (And no offense meant to followers of [Henry James](http://tinyurl.com/9sj62kh "\"The Real Thing\" short story"), either.) Nobody, not even the artists who afford us this vision, can live seeing “face to face” nonstop. That would be like looking straight into the sun all the time.

Alastair brought up Harold Pinter earlier. And Pinter for me remains a shocking playwright, many decades after he first baffled and alienated audiences and critics. I was rattled by [“The Homecoming”](http://theater.nytimes.com/2007/12/17/theater/reviews/17home.html "Review of \"The Homecoming\" ") when I first read it as a teenager, and I continue to react that way every time I see it staged.

What gets to me, every time, isn’t just the obvious sexual appropriation of one man’s wife by his father and brothers. It’s the sense that I’m watching an X-ray of a family, and seeing the subterranean violence, raw sexual impulses and primal urges for power that animate it. Yet all this dark savagery has been given a perfectly naturalistic form, so you’re seeing text and subtext in one instant. That double-vision coherence has, for me at least, an extraordinary beauty.

O’Neill’s “Long Day’s Journey Into Night,” a far more conventional play in many ways, has the same effect on me. It possesses the same searing, cruel clarity about how family members have the power to wound one another like no one else. And, yes, I will always be shocked by “King Lear” and “Oedipus Rex” — and by certain movies by Ingmar Bergman and David Lynch and Jean-Luc Godard. I was shocked by[Paul Thomas Anderson’s new movie, “The Master.”](http://movies.nytimes.com/2012/09/14/movies/review-the-master-from-paul-thomas-anderson.html "Review of \"The Master\" ")

But it doesn’t have to be brutal art. There’s a part of me that’s always shocked by the transcendent harmonies of [“The Marriage of Figaro.”](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_oKU94kxv-o "Overture to \"The Marriage of Figaro\" ") It too knocks the breath out of me. Shock is inherent in art that makes us see or sense what we don’t see or sense every day, which for me is a fair definition of the function of art. I think great art hurts, even as it gives the most pleasure.

## Oct. 3**What Frightens Horror Directors?**

#### By ERIK PIEPENBURG

![Image 4](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2012/10/03/arts/shock-horror/shock-horror-custom1.jpg)

Gunnar Hansen as Leatherface in “Texas Chainsaw Massacre,” the 1974 film by Tobe Hooper. 

To say a work of art shocks for shock’s sake is often a pejorative statement. Not when the work in question is a horror film. More than in any other corner of the pop-culture world, a horror film is expected to shock an audience. Like roller coaster enthusiasts craving a rush, horror fans thrill at watching a masked psychopath (or ghost or alien or clown) kill off his victims in graphic and revolting ways. Want to see real terror in a horror director’s eyes? Say that his (or her) film isn’t shocking enough.

The New York Times recently spoke to four directors from the new and old schools of cinematic fear making: John Carpenter, the director of horror classics like [“Halloween”](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k2DWutxndgk "\"Halloween\" trailer") (1978) and “The Fog” (1980); Tobe Hooper, whose films include [“The Texas Chainsaw Massacre”](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vs3981DoINw "A trailer") (1974) and “Poltergeist” (1982); James Wan, whose [“Saw”](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lVTN-0IN5N4 "\"Saw\" trailer") (2004) spawned the “torture porn” mini-genre; and Adam Rehmeier, whose film [“The Bunny Game”](https://www.nytimes.com/2012/09/16/movies/rodleen-getsic-in-the-horror-film-the-bunny-game.html "Article about \"The Bunny Game\" ") (2012) was banned in Britain because of its depictions of extreme violence. These are excerpts from the conversations.

_WHAT SHOCKED YOU AS A CHILD?_

**JOHN CARPENTER:** There was a movie in 1958 called [“The Fly”](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5w4BqxL7WZ0 "Trailer for \"The Fly\" ") with Vincent Price. There’s a scene where the wife of the scientist who’s gone through a transition pulls the hood off, and you see he has a fly head. Oh my God. Popcorn went flying. I see it now, and I affectionately look at it. It’s a cheesy fly mask.

**TOBE HOOPER:** Seeing [“Frankenstein,”](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f_d_1QLbmQw "\"Frankenstein\" the movie") and the idea of Frankenstein. I was taken by my parents to a midnight screening where they promised Frankenstein in person, which would have been someone made up with a mask on. I was sure he was going to get me. I had to leave the theater. I didn’t see the film until later. The idea of someone being brought back from the grave piecemeal was shocking. Not that the film is terribly scary, but at that time ambience went a long way.

**JAMES WAN:** A film that I saw at a young age that scared me would be [“Poltergeist.”](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8hQkBLrd1rE "Trailer for \"Poltergeist\" ") The sequence with [the boy staring at the clown doll](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=56zYh57OEoc "Scene from \"Poltergeist\" ") next to him was very frightening. I remember very well that I was so caught up in the suspense that I found myself trying to hide behind the chair in front of me. That had a huge impact on me. I think I was about 7.

[Video 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=56zYh57OEoc)

_WHY IS SHOCK SO IMPORTANT TO THE HORROR FILM GENRE?_

**CARPENTER**: It’s all a part of the fun, the roller coaster ride of scaring people. Every once in a while you want a jolt, something that gets you going. Go back to 1931 and “Frankenstein.” When the monster appeared, there were three or four cuts right to his face. At the time that was a big jolt. People hadn’t seen anything like that before. Move forward to 1957, and there was a similar reveal in “The Curse of Frankenstein,” where there’s a really fast dolly into his face. Whoa. What a big shock. Shock moves along through culture and history. It’s not everything, but it is important to the genre.

**ADAM REHMEIER:** I think people love that adrenaline rush. It feels good but it’s also safe and controlled. James Wan’s “[Insidious”](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E1YbOMDI59k "Trailer for \"Insidious\" ") is a good example. There’s a scene where [a demon is over Patrick Wilson’s shoulder](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LNLnkGu8mEQ "Scene from \"Insidious\" "). It sends a shiver through you. It feels amazing. Most films don’t give you that excitement, or have much of an effect on your body.

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LNLnkGu8mEQ)

_HOW HAVE HORROR FILMS CHANGED?_

**CARPENTER:** Today there’s a genre of movie, the found-footage thing [like the [“Paranormal Activity”](http://www.paranormalmovie.com/ "Trailer for \"Paranormal Activity\" ") movies]. What it is is low budget. It’s a way to make a bunch of money for the producers. Horror films go through stages where they get harder, and they soften up again. By that I mean how much is revealed, how much is explicit. It constantly evolves.

**WAN:** I think that today’s audiences are more jaded. They’ve seen so much. Today’s kids are so inundated. It’s getting harder and trickier to try and shock someone, to surprise someone to make them shake in their boots. But that’s not a bad thing. As a filmmaker you have to step up your game and find new ways to reach out to people.

_WHAT SHOCKS YOU TODAY?_

**HOOPER:** In London I saw a play called [“Ghost Stories.”](http://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/theatre-dance/reviews/ghost-stories-lyric-hammersmith-london-1918303.html "Review of \"Ghost Stories\" ") I was really surprised to jump, to be affected and most particularly to be involved with the characters in a theater in the West End. That was truly my last really scary adventure. I was surprised that without the use of close-ups or anything other than the proscenium that it was incredibly affecting. The important thing is not to overexplain it or completely resolve it, but to let you leave the theater still thinking about it and have you figure it out yourself. At its best that’s what cinema does and should do.

**REHMEIER:** I love true crime. You can’t write something as good as it really happened. That’s what disturbs me the most: what humans do to each other. Like [the French film] [“Irreversible.”](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OU-ZOHeWLkU "Trailer for \"Irreversible\" ") What was equally as brutal as the infamous rape scene was the scene where he confronts the guy he believes raped his girlfriend, and bashes him with the fire extinguisher. It was one of the most brutal things I’ve seen in cinema. It leveled me.

**CARPENTER:** What shocks me is not so much works of art, although I did watch something years ago by Georges Franju called [“The Blood of Beasts,”](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QFAUA8_mfXs "Video of \"The Blood of Beasts\" ") a documentary on French slaughterhouses where animals are rendered into food. That’s shocking. It’s hard to watch. That’s one kind of shock, a shock to your sense of civility. Real life is shocking to me, what is said and what is done. If you look at Syria, that’s shocking, the inhumanity, the debasement of our better human qualities. This is not something new. Art can transform you, but it can’t shock you like that can shock you.

## Oct. 2**Maggie Nelson on the Limitations of Shock**

#### By JENNIFER SCHUESSLER

![Image 5](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2012/10/02/arts/nelson/nelson-articleInline.jpg)Harry Dodge Maggie Nelson.

Over the past two weeks in this space, readers, critics and artists have been asking whether art can still shock. But what’s so great about shock, anyway? In her book [“The Art of Cruelty: A Reckoning,”](https://www.nytimes.com/2011/07/17/books/review/book-review-the-art-of-cruelty-by-maggie-nelson.html "Review of \"The Art of Cruelty\" ") published last year to wide acclaim, the critic Maggie Nelson examined the “shock and awe” doctrine that has governed so much of the last century’s art, arguing that it has too often let artists off the hook for the less than edifying reactions their work may provoke.

In a recent e-mail conversation, Ms. Nelson, who teaches at California Institute of the Arts, talked about the difference between criticism and moralism, women’s ways of shocking, and a few things that have made her own jaw drop — in a good way. These are excerpts from the conversation.

**Q.** Your book questions the idea that art, by representing the cruelties of the world, can (to quote [the film director Michael Haneke](https://www.nytimes.com/2007/09/23/magazine/23haneke-t.html?pagewanted=all "Profile of Michael Haneke")) “rape the viewer into independence.” What’s wrong with this “shock and awe” doctrine?

**A.** I find this doctrine dreadful because I’m not an ends-justify-the-means person. That is to say: if there’s a kind of worthwhile independence brought about by a rape, even if a figurative one, you can count me out. Haneke is speaking metaphorically, but metaphors matter.

I like it when artists face up to the unmanageable effects of their work, rather than try to hide those unmanageable effects behind comments like, “My work isn’t cruel — it’s the world that’s cruel.” I don’t need artists to be moralizers or physicians. I’d rather that we admit that depicting shocking, violent or cruel behaviors always provokes difficult questions about voyeurism, sadism, masochism and titillation, and that those provocations cannot always stay under the artist’s control.

**Q.**[Andres Serrano’s “Piss Christ,”](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piss_Christ "Background about \"Piss Christ\" ") the 1987 photograph that helped lead to a campaign to shut down the National Endowment for the Arts, returned to a New York gallery last week, and some public moralists [tried to stage a rerun of the culture wars](https://www.nytimes.com/2012/09/29/nyregion/catholic-leader-turned-away-at-exhibit-he-deemed-offensive.html "Article about protests"). But you argue that in the decades since then, the question of whether images can lead to injury has been posed most often by “art’s trashy cousin, mass media.” What has changed?

**A.** There’s a lot out there that can shock — in high art, on TV, on the news — and then there’s the Internet, where you can find nearly anything you want (or don’t want) to see with a few clicks of a mouse. It never makes much sense to me when people say, “Nothing’s shocking,” because shock isn’t about content as much as it is about context.

More importantly, images don’t typically leap into causing outrage or shock on their own. Whether it’s “Piss Christ” or “Innocence of Muslims,” certain forces are hard at work circulating the offending agent and fanning the flames. Even back in the bad old days of the culture wars, outrage over “Piss Christ” (or over Robert Mapplethorpe, or [Karen Finley](https://www.nytimes.com/1990/05/21/arts/review-art-effects-of-men-s-desires-on-the-lives-of-women.html?ref=karenfinley "Article about Karen Finley"), etc.) was ginned up by particular politicians to serve specific political goals that way preceded Serrano’s urge to submerge a crucifix in his urine.

**Q.** In the book you talk about your dismay at the marketing of [the torture-porn movie “Captivity,”](https://www.nytimes.com/2007/06/25/movies/25horr.html "Article about the marketing") and also at the “Tipper-Gore-esque” voice you imagine yourself voicing your complaints in. Do debates over censorship and free speech tend to cloud our perceptions of the issues you raise?

![Image 6](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2012/10/02/arts/shock-captivity/shock-captivity-custom1.jpg)

After Dark Films

Elisha Cuthbert in “Captivity.” 

**A.** I think it’s pretty clear from my book that I am a big First Amendment supporter, and I rarely, if ever, think censorship is the answer. But you’re right, I was trying to make the point that sometimes the “should it be permitted” conversation mows over the more subtle conversations that can unfold when you start off assuming an ample right to free expression. With “Captivity,” I was not interested in whether such movies should be made, but rather in how “free speech” intersects with corporate interests and public space. Billboard campaigns make that tension clear, in that billboards appear to occupy the so-called public sphere but are very clearly bought and sold by private parties.

**Q.** At the end of the book you mention a long list of artists whose work “dismantles, boycotts, ignores, destroys, takes liberty with or at least pokes fun at” the idea that shock leads to enlightenment. Most of the artists on your list are women. Have women found a different, more fruitful route to shock?

**A.** I’d love to claim for my putative gender a claim on more fruitful art making, but I don’t think such a generalization could stand. I will say, however, that men have had the run of the board for hundreds of years now in terms of art history, so we’ve seen and heard a lot of what they have to say. I don’t know any women who would nominate the nine-minute rape scene in the [2002 movie “Irreversible”](http://movies.nytimes.com/movie/review?res=9e07efdd133ff934a35750c0a9659c8b63 "Review of film.") as an avant-garde tour de force — the whole sex/violence thing may remain horrifying, but it is not novel.

The shock of work by certain female artists often lies in their capacity to say things the culture has a hard time hearing or hasn’t yet heard. (Think of Jesse Helms, who could only perceive Karen Finley as [“that chocolate-smeared woman”](http://www.news.harvard.edu/gazette/2002/02.14/06-finley.html "Article about Karen Finley"); that her self-smearing was in part a protest against women being treated like excrement was lost on him.) My favorite work by certain women (and men, and everyone in-between) often makes my mouth drop open — not from being offended, but out of wonder: you can say that? you can do that?

**Q.** What have you encountered recently that made your mouth drop open that way?

**A.** Lee Miller’s [1930 prints of breasts on plates](http://www.flickr.com/photos/missmarissalynn/6914739483/ "Lee Milller photos") (“Untitled (Severed Breast from Radical Mastectomy)”); she stole the breasts from a hospital after a friend’s surgery! Carolee Schneemann’s [“Infinity Kisses,”](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_m4wuJH4M8I "\"Infinity Kisses\" video") which captures a multiyear, erotic engagement Schneemann had with various cats.

[Video 4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_m4wuJH4M8I)

[Michelle Tea’s blog “Getting Pregnant with Michelle Tea,”](http://www.xojane.com/family/getting-pregnant-michelle-tea "Michelle Tea’s blog"), in which Tea gamely ponders the vicissitudes of her discharge and orders black-market Clomid from Mexico, amongst other things. [Dodie Bellamy’s “The Buddhist,”](http://girlslikegiants.wordpress.com/2012/04/17/an-interview-with-dodie-bellamy/ "Interview with Dodie Bellamy") which graphically describes having sex as a middle-aged woman, perhaps one of the final frontiers. Eileen Myles’s catalog (in [“Inferno”](http://www.orbooks.com/catalog/inferno-a-poets-novel/)) of various vaginas she’s encountered over the years — a piece Myles says even Vice magazine initially had cold feet about publishing. [Kara Walker’s psychosexual fantasia](http://learn.walkerart.org/karawalker "Web site for Kara Walker") against the backdrop of American slavery. The tender brutality in the work of [Harry Dodge](https://www.nytimes.com/2008/03/02/arts/design/02fink.html "Review of Harry Dodge"). All of [Luther Price](http://whitney.org/Exhibitions/2012Biennial/LutherPrice "Luther Price Web page"). The benevolent audacity of [Annie Sprinkle](http://artsbeat.blogs.nytimes.com/2011/07/01/reviewer-spotlight-annie-sprinkle-on-sex-art-and-activism/ "Interview with Annie Sprinkle") and [C A Conrad](http://www.poetryfoundation.org/article/237974 "Web site of CA Conrad’s work").

**Q.** Are there any shock artists you find particularly overrated?

**A.** Probably most. Truth be told, I’m not much into shock. While writing this book, people kept telling me about the most God-awful things, and so it’s kind of a relief to have stopped the flow. I agree with John Waters when he says, “It’s easy to shock, but it’s much harder to surprise with wit.” While some of the work I’ve mentioned above may strike others as shocking, to me, it’s mostly just smart, original people expressing blessedly fresh truths.

_An earlier version of this post misstated the title of a work by Eileen Myles. It is “Inferno,” not “The Inferno.”_

## Oct. 1**Critics’ Forum: Pop Music**

_Three New York Times critics — Jon Pareles, Ben Ratliff and Jon Caramanica— chat about the role of shock in pop music._

**JON PARELES** Face it: In popular music, shock is no taboo to be daringly broken. It’s a three-in-one winner: an attention-getter, a posture of rebellion, a jolt of pleasure. Dissonance either resolves to consonance or starts to sound pretty good in itself. Syncopation is a series of controlled microshocks that turn into a reason to move. Noise is an irritant that quickly reconfigures from a surprise into a landmark or an identifier, an instant way to recognize a song. Lyrics that try to shock via profanity, sex, politics or hate are a self-defeating arms race, exhausting their novelty fast.

**BEN RATLIFF** All art depends on some relationship to sincerity, as well as a loop from artist to audience and back to artist again. Historically, pop music is a short-loop, disingenuous art. (Classical music is a long-loop ingenuous art. Jazz is always the middle, being flexible.)

It’s a very basic posture for pop music to be Groucho Marx. It’s always looking for another [Margaret Dumont](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=H3FZ_jtDMVg "Margaret Dumont in \"Duck Soup\" ") to flatter and then upset within five seconds. The thing is, Margaret is a construct. Most people aren’t truly that shocked by dissonance, nakedness, heresy, abnormal psychology. They’ve probably experienced it before in their own lives and families and atmospheres. When they react to [Tyler, the Creato](https://www.nytimes.com/2010/11/13/arts/music/13odd.html "Article about Tyler, the Creator")r’s violent images, or [Britney Spears’s Catholic-schoolgirl video](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C-u5WLJ9Yk4 "Britney Spears in \"Baby One More Time\" ") or [the Sex Pistols](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8z2M_hpoPwk "\"God Save the Queen\" video"), they’re enacting a role, as a way of taking part in the fast loop.

![Image 7](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2010/11/13/arts/odd/odd-articleLarge.jpg)

Josh Haner/The New York Times

A bare-chested Tyler, the Creator and other members of the hip-hop crew Odd Future. 

The reaction isn’t necessarily true, though it’s important, if mostly vestigial at this point. But there are other kinds of shocks in our discipline, aren’t there? Shocks that aren’t explicitly about primitivism or breaking the social contract?

**JON CARAMANICA** I agree that outrage is something that’s enacted more than felt, but that’s far larger than pop. There’s something hopelessly middle class about shock. To be shocked is to be privileged. Or better, to be shocked is to assert privilege, to declare oneself above the stain. Shock is what happens when people step out of their comfort zones into the gap between delivery and expectation.

The goal — my goal, at least — is to wipe oneself clear of expectation. I’ll never recreate the shock of my first exposure to, say, [Slick Rick’s “Treat Her Like a Prostitute”](http://www.last.fm/music/Slick+Rick/_/Treat+Her+Like+A+Prostitute "Audio of the song") — a formative shock, in many ways — but then again, I’m not 13 anymore. When I was younger, the pop sneer meant a lot to me. (The real middle-finger-up move would have probably been to get into Morton Subotnick and psychotropics, but I wasn’t that advanced.)

I realize now that everything is a pose, and I don’t think that’s just because my nerve endings have been dulled. Increasingly, the shocks I experience are in the body — the volcanic, stomach-quaking rumble of a [Godspeed! You Black Emperor show](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5gmxBRkQd70 "Video from a concert"), the triumphant muscle flexes of a Lex Luger or Young Chop beat, or the time I had to leave a [Sigur Ros](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zr_MJAOyOeU "Sigur Ros video") concert because the sound was squeezing tears from my eyes. The mind adapts, but the body remains raw.

[Video 5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GZFzJr9NnPE)

**MR. PARELES** Or maybe to feel shockproof is to be even more privileged. As in, from my lofty domain I recognize the unreliable-narrator literary strategies of your death-metal bands like [Morbid Angel](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UYdfsZRURF0 "Video of Morbid Angel"); I register all the qualifiers and distancing mechanisms that Eminem or Tyler, the Creator bring to their smorgasbords of gross-outs; I can savor the ugly beauty of a distortion blast. Outrage would mean reinforcing the feedback loop, joining the fray, while we can just survey it knowingly from our intellectual heights, our figurative skybox seats. But that perspective is a little too jaded. We can still be jarred.

I got into this racket earlier than you two. And I can remember, in my high school days, when hearing hundreds of thousands of people shout back [Country Joe McDonald’s “Fish Cheer”](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_xFn8O9TTr0 "Video of the song") with a stronger four-letter word — this was the Woodstock Festival in 1969 — was indeed a shock. But it was a freeing one — from radio-regulated vocabulary and all-too-polite discourse — and how quaint it now seems to get all that from one cheap cussword.

Later came other revelatory shocks from [Parliament-Funkadelic](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jJvjWh2Vhu4 "Video of the band"), wandering around the Mothership in glitter and diapers; from [Glenn Branca](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xdLhRB4dJJI "Video of Glenn Branca"), [the Notekillers](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sD4KkvuPJC4 "Video of the Notekillers in concert") and [Sonic Youth](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tdeTQPgh9SE "Video of Sonic Youth in concert"), making drone guitars summon killer swarms of overtones to shock previously unused ear receptors; from Slayer and Metallica triggering near-fibrillation, and from Nine Inch Nails nailing down feelings previously unnamed.

[Video 6](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JPkaiW2ZYnE)

But those weren’t the kind of shocks that would also arrive soon enough, the shock effects that make you feel sullied or complicit with sleaze: blood-spattered Alice Cooper tomfoolery or the smooth Dr. Dre productions selling [Snoop Doggy Dogg’](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IZpEq4wtKNI "Snoop Doggy Dogg video")s callous macho materialism. There’s shock that simply baits the audience, and shock that opens perceptions, and — just to keep things interesting — no clear boundary between them.

**MR. RATLIFF** If we’re talking about ourselves, the privilege might be all the music that we hear, and our permanent readiness to contextualize music as soon as we hear it. Broad knowledge — even the kind you can create for yourself right this minute with deft Internet magic re Tyler, the Creator; Young Chop; and the Notekillers — kind of nullifies shock. That’s why we’re traveling back in our minds to when we were young, a k a when we were unaware.

You have got to be right, Jon P., about shock being perhaps a more frequent reaction in the ’60s and ’70s. But was it because nobody had ever done anything comparable before? Or was it because it was harder to get information then? Would Jimi Hendrix shock you in 1966 if you’d stood in front of Johnny Guitar Watson’s amp in 1954 or had been able to get a sense of that on YouTube? I know, it’s boring, this nothing-new-under-the-sun thing. But we have access to so much more now.

Couple more thoughts. A lot of people talk about “the first note” or “the first chord” of something really shattering them: friends have told me about this regarding their first experiences seeing [Hendrix](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UVfoDO05xWM&list=AL94UKMTqg-9BS-GQFJJC4rwB8PeWMXx8M&index=2&feature=plcp "Jimi Hendrix in concert"), [Coltrane](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0I6xkVRWzCY "Video of John Coltrane"), [Mahavishnu Orchestra](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MtSIEkPqVgk "Video of Mahavisnu Orchestra"), [My Bloody Valentine](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t0dJqlvOSq4 "\"Sometimes\" by My Bloody Valentine"). I’ve experienced it, too. That seems like a genuine form of shock, the body-reaction kind.

[Video 7](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MtSIEkPqVgk)

I am sometimes shocked, if that’s the word, and I’m not sure it is, by performances that refuse to respect the conventions of performance: songs that never end, the performer coming into the audience, the constant breaks and side roads in some gospel and hip-hop shows. I’m shocked by generosity, by performers doing a lot more than they really need to, or producing a single note that is a lot truer than it has to be, or by working against their own interests and allowing silence. If pop is a game, all that stuff can seem like a saintly renouncing of the game, or an expansion of it.

**MR. CARAMANICA** But this is exactly why I think shock is a farce. By and large, we’re not talking about children, we’re talking about adults, some of whom are certainly sheltered, but the vast majority of whom have been shaped by their experiences with love and sex and violence and death and laughter and shame and anguish. Maybe they like keeping the resultant feelings locked up, and a chance encounter with a pop song can be an awkward reminder. (These days, the more deliberate provocations happen in the world of performance art, or even theater and dance, than in ours, I’d guess.) So there, pop’s not at fault; people are. Problem solved. Ha!

Fine, though. In the spirit of good sportsmanship, I’ll bite. I recently wrote about [an album by Waxahatchee](https://www.nytimes.com/2012/09/02/arts/music/allison-and-katie-crutchfield-twins-go-separate-ways.html?pagewanted=all "Jon Caramanica article"), the recording alias of Katie Crutchfield. When I first encountered the album, I couldn’t get through the whole thing in one sitting. It was spare, unfinished and disorientingly intimate — it felt scarred. It made my breathing irregular. It was as if I could feel the rupturing of the buffer zone around me, but I couldn’t do anything about it. The womb dissolved — a shock, for sure — but after a while, I became acclimated to the light sensitivity, the heightened tingle of touch. I was feeling things anew. A good shock.

**MR. PARELES** In the end, the sticking point may be that labeling something as shock is a way of belittling it: Oh, their whole intention is just to shock people. Certainly there’s enough of that around, and even in our happily vulgar mass culture, I don’t think we’ve seen the last calculated attempt to push people’s buttons in the crassest ways possible.

But I think that as popular-music critics, what we’ve come around to here is a different effect that we’re also calling shock: a swift kick in the preconceptions, a perceptual challenge that transforms itself into a revelation, a startling sound or song that remaps everything around it. Maybe we shouldn’t be calling that a shock. Maybe we should just call it artists at work.

## Sept. 28**Adam Rapp on Audience Reactions**

#### By JENNIFER SCHUESSLER

![Image 8](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2010/05/18/arts/18metal_CA0/18metal_CA0-custom1.jpg)Nicole Bengiveno/The New York Times Adam Rapp.

In more than two dozen plays over two decades the New York playwright (and Pulitzer Prize finalist) [Adam Rapp](https://static01.nyt.com/packages/khtml/2006/02/09/theater/20060210_RAPP_AUDIOSS.html?ref=adamrapp "An audio interview") has presented a dark emotional realism fleshed out with generous doses of sex, violence and bodily fluids. In an e-mail conversation Mr. Rapp, whose new play, [“Through the Yellow Hour,”](http://theater.nytimes.com/2012/09/28/theater/reviews/adam-rapps-through-the-yellow-hour-at-rattlestick.html?ref=theater "Times review by Ben Brantley") just opened at New York’s Rattlestick Playwrights Theater, talks about the importance of kicking the audience in the shins, why it’s become harder to get a reaction out of audiences, and the scene that has most shocked him. These are excerpts from the conversation.

**Q.**[Admirers](http://bombsite.com/issues/95/articles/2819 "An interview with Adam Rapp") and [detractors](http://artsbeat.blogs.nytimes.com/2011/10/07/theater-talkback-for-one-critic-its-a-rapp/ "Charles Isherwood on Adam Rapp") of your work alike have cited its visceral, confrontational aesthetic. Is shocking the audience something you deliberately seek to do?

**A.** Early in my career I was really interested in putting actions onstage that I’d never seen before. I would imagine a moment that would be almost impossible to pull off, like someone urinating, or shooting up with insulin and leaving the needle dangling in his side. This excited me simply because when you encounter these kinds of moments, and they’re executed well, the audience likely forgets they’re sitting in a theater. That’s always been my goal: to make people get so lost in the play they think they’ve actually happened upon something. The greatest sin in the theater is boredom.

**Q.** Are there any particular playwrights who showed you what these kinds of moments might look like?

**A.** In my early 20s I was reading plays by [Edward Bond](http://www.edwardbond.org/ "Web site for Edward Bond"), [Sarah Kane](http://topics.nytimes.com/topics/reference/timestopics/people/k/sarah_kane/index.html "Articles about Sarah Kane"), [Caryl Churchill](http://topics.nytimes.com/top/reference/timestopics/people/c/caryl_churchill/index.html "Articles about Caryl Churchill") and [Harold Pinter](http://theater.nytimes.com/2008/12/26/theater/26pinter.html?ref=haroldpinter "Harold Pinter obituary"). I wanted to reach the same level of intensity that I encountered in their work because I was rarely experiencing this when I went to the theater. Everything seemed so safe and presentational. I was excited by the possibility of changing the nervous system of the audience, and I still am. But now, many plays later, I find that whether it’s sex, drugs, urination or violence, not only does it have to be well executed, but it has to be organically justified by the narrative. Otherwise it will feel gratuitous, and the audience will lean away from the play, and that kind of death is almost as bad as boredom.

![Image 9](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2012/09/28/arts/28shock-rapp/28shock-rapp-articleLarge.jpg)

Sara Krulwich/The New York Times

Christopher Denham, left, Gary Wilmes and Lisa Joyce in Mr. Rapp’s play “Red Light Winter.”

**Q.** Has it become harder to push an audience past its comfort zone?

**A.** I think it is harder to shock audiences than it used to be because now one can go on the Internet and have a very intimate experience with sex and violence. The immediate access is sort of stunning. Today I’m less interested in writing toward a shocking moment than in writing a good play, but I still think getting an audience out of their comfort zone is hugely important. I refuse to see theater simply as entertainment. It should challenge an audience and push them away from what TV generally gives them. And sometimes a good punch to the stomach or a kick to the shins can be a very good thing. The English playwright Howard Brenton once said, “Theater’s a real bear pit.” I believe in this very much.

**Q.** Is there a play you recall as having particularly shocked you?

**A.** One of the most shocking moments I’ve seen in the theater involved a letter. In Martin McDonagh’s [“The Beauty Queen of Leenane,”](https://www.nytimes.com/1998/02/27/movies/theater-review-a-gasp-for-breath-inside-an-airless-life.html "Review of \"The Beauty Queen of Leenane") Maureen, the 40-year-old spinster who is living with Mag, her embittered mother, receives a love letter from Pato, a middle-aged construction worker. Maureen isn’t home when the letter arrives, and after Mag is left alone with it for a few minutes she starts the stove. We think she’s going to make herself some tea, but she winds up throwing the letter into the oven. The moment was so shocking — the snapping shut of that oven door — that the Broadway audience gasped and cried as if they were watching a slasher moment in a horror movie. McDonagh had done such a good job front-loading Maureen’s loneliness and frustration, and this last chance at love was destroyed by one simple swift action. It broke my heart. and I had knots in my stomach for the rest of the play.

## Sept. 27**Critics’ Forum: The Visceral Reaction**

_Four New York Times critics — Roberta Smith, Ben Brantley, A. O. Scott and Alastair Macaulay— are chatting about the role of shock in art: how it works, how it has changed and why it’s still necessary. Jennifer Schuessler moderates._

**JENNIFER SCHUESSLER, REPORTER:** Ben writes that “shock, if we’re still using that word, is visceral.” Alastair, I think you’re the one who got us talking about semantics. Would you agree? And what are some of the shocks (jolts? surprises?) you’ve felt most deeply in your gut?

![Image 10](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2012/09/27/arts/27shock-pinter/27shock-pinter-articleInline.jpg)Carl de Souza/Associated Press Harold Pinter in 2007.

**ALASTAIR MACAULAY, CHIEF DANCE CRITIC:** Shock is, as Ben says, visceral; but it’s also entirely contextual. The greatest shock I recall in over 34 years as a critic lay in a radical non sequitur. It was the [world premiere of Harold Pinter’s “Ashes to Ashes”](https://www.nytimes.com/1996/09/25/style/25iht-lon.t_3.html "International Herald Tribune article from 1996.") (1996), a play for one male-female couple, Rebecca and Devlin. Rebecca is recalling her relationship with an authority figure in a state where genocide occurred. At one point she describes how she once watched this man she loved walk down a row of screaming mothers and tear from them the bundles that contained their babies. A silence follows. Then Devlin replies: “Did you see Kim and the kids?” On first experience of the play that nonanswer was shocking — it felt like walking straight into a wall — because Devlin sounded so callously indifferent to Rebecca’s appalling testimony. As I revisited the play over weeks and months, I came to understand that the opposite was also true. Rebecca’s testimony is a form of delusion or psychosis, and Devlin’s question about Kim and the kids is an attempt (successful, in the short term) to draw her back into the everyday world she knows.

Some of the shock of his line endures, though, like an extreme discord in music, it is on so strikingly different a wavelength. Rebecca, however confused about her own life, is attuned to some of the great horrors of recent times. At no point does Devlin show the least largeness of spirit. And so it becomes implicit that this fascist figure in Rebecca’s mind is her nightmare version of Devlin, her own petty domestic tyrant. As a meeting of the political and the personal it remains for me a breathtaking play: not Pinter’s most perfect but his greatest.

Devlin’s line, however, isn’t a front-page shock. I remember how two London critics were so aghast after the world premiere of [Sarah Kane’s “Blasted”](http://theater.nytimes.com/2008/11/06/theater/06blas.html?ref=sarahkane&pagewanted=all "Times article on the play by Patrick Healy.") that, talking outside the theater afterward, they decided to propose to their newspapers that their outrage should be front-page rather than arts-page. Whether or not they were right — one of those critics died a few years later, the other has since recanted about Kane — this reminds us that shock isn’t solely a spontaneous reaction.

After the first feeling of being taken aback, we then make decisions. Outrage isn’t just instinctive; it too is an act, a form of performance. The people who booed and heckled during the premiere of Stravinsky’s “Rite” decided to fight; and probably Diaghilev had spent weeks preparing Paris for battle. (He well knew how proud Paris was of its tradition of scandalous first nights.)

Usually we in the West decide these days to play it cool, even blasé, about [displays of nakedness](https://www.nytimes.com/2012/08/19/arts/dance/nakedness-in-dance-taken-to-extremes.html?pagewanted=all "Times article by Alastair Macaulay"), sexual deviation, musical loudness and discord. Cannibalism, genocide, torture, heresy: these are among the chief shockers today. Pinter at the time of “Ashes to Ashes” was friends with Sarah Kane; I’ve often wondered whether his play wasn’t his way of taking the horrors of her “Blasted” and connecting them to the shocks of his own personal force fields.

At the moment such a battle — the shock of heresy — is [being fought about “Innocence of Muslims.”](http://topics.nytimes.com/top/reference/timestopics/subjects/i/innocence_of_muslims_riots/index.html "Topics page.") I remember not only the brouhaha about “The Satanic Verses” but also [“Monty Python’s Life of Brian,”](http://movies.nytimes.com/movie/review?res=9900E2DD1339E732A25754C1A96E9C946890D6CF "1979 Times review by Vincent Canby.") which in 1979 was made to sound the ultimate in bad taste.

[Video 8](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vVHhg67RVd4)

Now “Life of Brian” is a candidate for all-time best comedy, and its song [“Always Look on the Bright Side of Life”](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SJUhlRoBL8M "Trailer") has been recycled in the musical [“Monty Python’s Spamalot”](http://theater2.nytimes.com/2005/03/18/theater/reviews/18spam.html?incamp=article_popular_1&pagewanted=all&position= "Times review by Ben Brantley.") and even the recent closing Olympic ceremony. Some of the movie’s outrageous quality remains, but now we look forward to such impudence. Some of the clashing discords and once-unnerving sonorities in modernist music become pleasurable on revisiting; some of the obscurities in modernist poetry and drama become sensuous.

In 2008 the French-Algerian modern dancer [Rachid Ouramdane presented “Far...”,](https://www.nytimes.com/2008/05/10/arts/dance/10rach.html "Times review by Alastair Macaulay.") which was largely docudrama, to Dance Theater Workshop. The testimony of torture it presented on film was dismaying, but what took me most aback was the way he then danced — not in protest or grief but gently, as if numb. The dance, in context, was about not feeling but the mind’s withdrawal from feeling: post-traumatic stress in movement. Nobody could be outraged by such dancing. But that non sequitur effect, like “Did you see Kim and the kids?,” remains a major jolt to the senses.

![Image 11](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2008/05/10/arts/dance/rachid.jpg)

Julien Jourdes for The New York Times

Rachid Ouramdane performing “Far...” at Dance Theater Workshop. 

**BEN BRANTLEY, CHIEF THEATER CRITIC:**That’s a very shrewd point, Alastair, about shock being a matter of social choice, or even social collusion, especially these days when it often feels as if it’s been removed from our conditioned reflex system, at least in response to art. There’s also the sense that often art doesn’t make a straightforward statement. I think that’s generally true of great art, but now it seems to be the modus operandi for lesser art too.

What an artist says may be only a pose, after all, and how foolish we’d look if we took him or her literally or failed to see the invisible quotation marks. At the same time, we seem to take all public figures, whether politicians or movie stars, exactly at their words. It’s as if irony isn’t allowed to exist in public discourse, whereas it’s sine qua non in much art today.

## Sept. 26**Chuck Palahniuk on Transgressive Fiction**

#### By JENNIFER SCHUESSLER

![Image 12](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2012/09/27/arts/27shock-palahniuk/27shock-palahniuk-articleInline.jpg)Alfredo Aldai/European Pressphoto Agency Chuck Palahniuk.

Chuck Palahniuk shot to fame in 1999 with David Fincher’s [now-classic screen adaptation of his novel “Fight Club,”](https://www.nytimes.com/2009/11/08/movies/homevideo/08lim.html "Times article on the film by Dennis Lim.") an incendiary exploration of violence and masculine alienation that one critic, in a not atypical sentiment, denounced as “a film without a single redeeming quality, which may have to find its audience in hell.” Since then, in novels like “Choke,” “Rant” and “Snuff,” Mr. Palahniuk has continued to explore the outer limits of human behavior, delivering shocks that have divided the critics while inspiring [rabid fan devotion](http://chuckpalahniuk.net/ "The author’s Web site.") and more than a few public faintings. (Nearly 70 people had passed out at readings of [his story](http://chuckpalahniuk.net/features/shorts/guts "The story.") “Guts,” [he once boasted](http://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/books/3643352/67-people-fainted-as-I-read-my-horror-story.html).)

In a recent e-mail conversation, Mr. Palahniuk, whose novel [“Damned”](https://www.nytimes.com/2011/10/20/books/damned-by-chuck-palahniuk-review.html "Times review by Janet Maslin.") appears in paperback next week, talked about the future of transgressive fiction, his preferred self-cure for “short-term insanity” and the written word’s unique pathways to shock.

**Q.**You’ve been called a literary “shock jock” by fans and detractors alike. Is shocking readers something you deliberately set out to do?

**A.** It’s never my intention to offend a reader or listener; I’m too addicted to external approval. When I write, one of my basic goals is to preserve and communicate the incredible stories I hear from people, true stories from real people. By finding a common theme between several anecdotes, often told to me decades apart, I can create a collage of kinetic, visually bold images that combine to illustrate a bigger truth. When I take a year to write a story, I’m doing so because I find it emotionally moving. If you were to read that story every day for a year, you’d move past any initial shock and also find the heartbreak. Culture that’s harder to accept, initially, tends to be culture that lasts longer.

![Image 13](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2012/09/26/arts/26shock-palahniuk-book/26shock-palahniuk-book-articleInline.jpg)

**Q.**In [the documentary “Postcards From the Future”](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w1oSvg7OI0Q "A clip from the film.") (2003), you said that “transgressive fiction” died after Sept. 11, and that maybe it was time for social commentary in art to become “charming, seductive and entertaining.” Has transgressive fiction come back since then? Or has it become more difficult for art to be as shocking as the world itself?

**A.** “Transgressive fiction” has become an oxymoron. Almost all the dynamic, edgy storytellers have moved to film, and books have fallen into that twilight of pre-death where live theater limps along. The most successful books now serve us as sedatives, confirming the values and worldviews their readers already hold. They’re the books we read as sleeping pills at bedtime. When was the last book banned? Oh, how I miss the great book bonfires of my Christian youth! That’s when books had some power! When they had to be burned like witches.

**Q.** You have said that one of your goals in writing is to shock yourself. But how easy is it for other people to shock you?

**A.**To be honest, my best writing happens when I need some place to put my short-term insanity. And it’s a vast comfort when other people tell me secrets that put my suicide-watch moods into perspective. The sudden release of tension: the revelation that I’m not suffering alone, that everyone endures this, it occurs like the punch line of a joke. So much is resolved so quickly that I have to laugh or gasp. When people give me that gift I can’t wait to pay it forward and have that same wonderful effect on someone else.

[Video 9](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x9Huy-JP1xo)

**Q.**Several of your novels and stories have been turned into movies, and “Fight Club” has got to be on many people’s list of most shocking movie endings. Do you think it’s harder for a novel to have that kind of immediate visceral effect on the reader? Or does the written word have its own uniquely powerful paths to shock?

**A.** The key is to play to the strength of the medium. It’s easier to hide the ultimate truth in books and stories. It’s easier to create spectacle in films. In the novel “Fight Club” our last glimpse of the narrator is in “heaven” haggling with “God,” but the reader realizes it’s actually a mental hospital and a psychologist. Such a quiet ambiguous ending doesn’t serve an audience seated at the foot of a 100-foot-tall screen. The book tells an intimate, interior story. The film does what film does best. The two forms can coexist. David Fincher’s no dummy.

## Sept. 26**The Tie Between Comedy and Horror**

#### By JASON ZINOMAN

In a [stand-up set](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pqG0Ho1bDxA&feature=related) on Comedy Central in July, the comic Ben Kronberg made a distinction. “A bun in the oven is cute, but a baby in the oven is horrifying,” he said. Then he went a little further. “And if you get a really young girl pregnant, it’s like a bun in the [Easy-Bake Oven](http://www.hasbro.com/easy-bake/en_US/ "Easy-Bake Oven Web site"), because they come out all doughy and stuff.”

Both jokes got laughs, but only the second punch line received queasy gasps. (The creepy hand gesture that accompanied the word “doughy” may have had something to do with that stomach-turning reaction.) Mr. Kronberg is a sly oddball who tells well-sculptured jokes about abortion, disease and racism, but the most shocking are simply gross. Finishing this bit, he says: “I know: Eww.”

![Image 14](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2012/09/26/arts/shock-tosh/shock-tosh-articleInline.jpg)Barbara P. Fernandez for The New York Times Daniel Tosh.

The sick jokes that cause the biggest fuss these days push moral hot buttons. (See [Daniel Tosh](https://www.nytimes.com/2012/07/18/arts/television/when-the-comic-and-the-heckler-both-take-offense.html?pagewanted=all)’s rape joke.) But the more common ones, which you find everywhere from shock radio to “Bridesmaids,” appeal to the limitless appetite for eww. This comedy is often more silly than scandalous, disgusting than dark. Yet the gags can sometimes shock, their power deriving from surprise, excess and busting taboos. They overlap with an equally fertile element of the horror genre: [gore.](http://www.slate.com/articles/arts/culturebox/features/2011/how_to_fix_horror/part_iv_gore_is_good.html) Gross-out comedy is a cousin to the splatter film.

As I learned reporting [my book, “Shock Value: How a Few Eccentric Outsiders Gave Us Nightmares, Conquered Hollywood and Invented Modern Horror,”](https://www.nytimes.com/2011/07/11/books/shock-value-by-jason-zinoman-review.html "Times review by Ty Burr") the line between horror and comedy has long been blurry. Alfred Hitchcock called “Psycho” a comedy. Tobe Hooper expected people to laugh at “The Texas Chainsaw Massacre.” In a similar fashion, comedians are famously dark and obsessed with death.

[Video 10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=285ImXTYdsg)

The relationship between vulgar humor and repulsive horror is particularly close. It’s no accident that after helping pioneer the slasher movie with the 1974 sorority house thriller [“Black Christmas,”](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=08U_JOv-6_Y) the Canadian director Bob Clark went on to make [“Porky’s,”](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0084522/) the dirty godfather of the raunchy teenage sex comedy. While the past few decades have made these movies seem far less shocking than they once were, these commercial genres still trade on shock.

And the pacing is similar. Just look at audiences watching them. They start relaxed, then become increasingly tense as the action builds, and then after the big reveal, be it a joke or a kill, the viewers’ anxiety dissipates audibly with either a laugh or a gasp. At scary movies the first thing audiences typically do after screaming is laugh at themselves. While explicit material may turn off some, others become more alert.

So much art washes over us, or is predictable enough that it requires only partial attention. Say what you want about the image of a doughy baby, but it gets your attention. George A. Romero, [the horror auteur](https://www.nytimes.com/2008/02/10/movies/10onst.html "Feature about George A. Romero") of “Night of the Living Dead” and more, describes gore’s purpose as a “slap in the face, a wake-up call, an alarm clock.”

But the artists who are out only to ring an alarm waste an opportunity. The best ones exploit it to make the kind of artistic statement that you couldn’t get away with in a more restrained movie. There is an art to a [good flatulence joke](https://www.nytimes.com/2012/04/28/arts/one-man-two-guvnors-is-born-of-a-long-tradition.html), and anyone who has seen a murder choreographed by Dario Argento or Brian De Palma knows that some assaults on good taste are in service of a refined aesthetic.

The varieties of shock in horror and comedy can seem endless. For many people the excitement of gross-outs is in the excess. If you look at the early movies of Peter Jackson or Sam Raimi, like [“Dead Alive”](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BnCfUpw-i7A) and [“The Evil Dead,”](http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dtsK7skqk9U) they are full of blood baths that are [strikingly beautiful](http://www.slate.com/articles/arts/culturebox/features/2011/how_to_fix_horror/part_iv_gore_is_good.html), yet also laughably ridiculous. Comic or scary gore can have a playfulness that aims for the gentlest of shocks. Martin McDonagh’s plays (notably [“A Skull in Connemara”](http://theater.nytimes.com/mem/theater/treview.html?res=9802e3d71539f930a15751c0a9679c8b63 "Ben Brantley review") and “[The Lieutenant of Inishmore”](http://theater2.nytimes.com/2006/02/28/theater/reviews/28inis.html "Ben Brantley review")) deliver tougher jolts that culminate in over-the-top scenes that manage to be both funny and menacing.

One of the most shocking comedies I’ve ever seen was “Billy the Mime,” in which [Steven Banks](http://theater.nytimes.com/2010/11/28/theater/28banks.html "Article about Steven Banks") took the most minimalist art form and injected it with gratuitous immorality. At the New York International Fringe Festival, he superbly [performed](http://theater.nytimes.com/2006/08/19/theater/19frin.html?pagewanted=print) a series of impossibly obscene vignettes without a word or prop. He dramatized scenes involving an altar boy and a priest, an abortion and the plotting and executing of the attacks on Sept. 11. Part of the shock here was in setting expectations. These sketches start light, silly, benign. After all, it’s _mime_, the cheesiest art form around, right? Then Mr. Banks skillfully ups the ante, taking audiences places they did not expect or probably want to go. Its tastelessness becomes its own pitch-black joke. And the realization that you laughed at it so heartily might be the most shocking part of the show.

## Sept. 25**A Dance Critic’s Most Shocking Moment**

#### By ALASTAIR MACAULAY

How many historic nights in the theater were actually a lot less historic than history makes out? I have read numerous reviews — by critics French, American and British — of the triumphant 1990 return of [the original 1913 staging of “Le Sacre du Printemps”](https://www.nytimes.com/2012/09/16/arts/shock-me-if-you-can.html?pagewanted=all "Article about original staging") (“The Rite of Spring”) to the site of its premiere, the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées in Paris. I attended that performance, and my own memories are not of triumph.

This Joffrey Ballet production had had [its premiere in the United States in 1987](https://www.nytimes.com/1987/10/25/arts/the-joffrey-ballet-restores-nijinsky-s-rite-of-spring.html?pagewanted=all&src=pm "Article about Joffrey Ballet production"), with Millicent Hodson staging her version of Vaslav Nijinsky’s choreography, and Kenneth Archer reviving the designs of Nicholas Roerich.

[Video 11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jF1OQkHybEQ)

Now the Joffrey was bringing it back to Paris, where just then I happened to be passing through. It proved easy that morning to buy a ticket. The theater is on the Avenue Montaigne, where many of the most eminent fashion salons of Paris have their homes, and that was the evening of their autumn openings. Dior! Chanel! Saint Laurent! Lacroix! Le tout Paris, gorgeously arrayed, was on the avenue that night as I made my way to the performance.

The audience at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées was not unfashionable. My seat was toward the back of the second ring. I remember the frisson of curious anticipation around me. In what frame of mind do you watch the revival of a scandal of yesteryear?

It’s famous that the riotous reaction to Stravinsky’s music on the first night in 1913 occurred immediately and continuously. In 1990, however, the audience around me was politely bored. A delectably well-dressed couple sat in the center of the front row, trying hard but unsuccessfully to be thrilled; I can never forget the look of their physical deflation as their heads and spines sagged. After 10 or 15 minutes they rested their elegant heads sideways on the balcony’s edge, as if the choreography were a lullaby.

They were, nonetheless, good sports. As soon as the music stopped, and a curtain descended, they burst into eager applause, leapt to their feet and cried, “Bravo, bravo!” — while starting to beat a brisk retreat to the exit. Then it suddenly dawned on them that this was the end not of the ballet but merely of its first part. Their faces fell, though they did not stop applauding. After a quick, anxious consultation, they decided that departure was the best policy; they were not alone.

Those who stayed greeted the end of the ballet’s second half in much the same spirit. There were many cries of “Bravo,” but they came from people who had never once looked electrified by the dancing onstage. The great events in Parisian culture that night were happening elsewhere — on the very same avenue.
